**Test cases the backend runs**

**Test 1: Runs the walkthrough from the instructions** (visible)

```typescript
import { createHandler, loadConfig } from "./solution.js";

// The walkthrough from the instructions: defaults, then one evening of bookings on a 30 kg kiln.

const defaults = loadConfig({});
check.equal(
  { host: defaults.host, port: defaults.port, maxLoadKg: defaults.maxLoadKg },
  { host: "127.0.0.1", port: 8080, maxLoadKg: 60 },
  "loadConfig({}) uses the default host, port and load",
);

const handle = createHandler(loadConfig({ KILN_MAX_LOAD_KG: "30" }));

check.equal(
  handle({ method: "GET", path: "/health", body: undefined }),
  { status: 200, body: { status: "ok" } },
  "GET /health answers 200 with { status: \"ok\" }",
);

const ines = handle({
  method: "POST",
  path: "/firings",
  body: { member: "  Ines Duarte ", pieces: 6, weightKg: 12.5, cone: "6" },
});
check.equal(
  ines,
  { status: 201, body: { booking: { id: "B-1", member: "Ines Duarte", pieces: 6, weightKg: 12.5, cone: "6" } } },
  "the first valid booking is created as B-1 with the member's name trimmed",
);

const tomas = handle({
  method: "POST",
  path: "/firings",
  body: { member: "Tomas", pieces: 4, weightKg: 15, cone: "06" },
});
check.equal(tomas.status, 201, "a second booking that still fits is created");

const full = handle({
  method: "POST",
  path: "/firings",
  body: { member: "Wen", pieces: 2, weightKg: 5, cone: "10" },
});
const fullBody = full.body as { error: { code: string; message: string } };
check.equal(full.status, 409, "a booking that would overload the kiln is refused with 409");
check.equal(fullBody.error.code, "kiln_full", "the refusal carries the code kiln_full");
check.equal(typeof fullBody.error.message, "string", "every error has a message");

const invalid = handle({
  method: "POST",
  path: "/firings",
  body: { member: "Ade", pieces: 0, weightKg: 2, cone: "5" },
});
const invalidBody = invalid.body as { error: { code: string; details: { field: string }[] } };
check.equal(invalid.status, 400, "an invalid booking is refused with 400");
check.equal(invalidBody.error.code, "invalid_body", "the refusal carries the code invalid_body");
check.equal(
  invalidBody.error.details.map((detail) => detail.field),
  ["pieces", "cone"],
  "the details name every field with a problem, in order",
);

check.equal(
  handle({ method: "GET", path: "/firings", body: undefined }),
  {
    status: 200,
    body: {
      bookings: [
        { id: "B-1", member: "Ines Duarte", pieces: 6, weightKg: 12.5, cone: "6" },
        { id: "B-2", member: "Tomas", pieces: 4, weightKg: 15, cone: "06" },
      ],
      loadKg: 27.5,
      capacityKg: 30,
    },
  },
  "GET /firings lists the accepted bookings with the load and the capacity",
);
```

**Test 2: Reads configuration from the environment and reports every problem** (hidden)

```typescript
import { ConfigError, loadConfig, type Config } from "./solution.js";

function plain(config: Config): { host: string; port: number; maxLoadKg: number } {
  return { host: config.host, port: config.port, maxLoadKg: config.maxLoadKg };
}

function problemsOf(env: Record<string, string | undefined>, what: string): readonly string[] {
  const error = check.throws(() => loadConfig(env), `loadConfig refuses ${what}`, ConfigError);
  return (error as ConfigError).problems;
}

function variablesIn(problems: readonly string[]): string[] {
  return problems.map((problem) => problem.split(" ")[0] ?? "");
}

check.equal(
  plain(loadConfig({ KILN_HOST: " 0.0.0.0 ", KILN_PORT: " 9090 ", KILN_MAX_LOAD_KG: "72.5" })),
  { host: "0.0.0.0", port: 9090, maxLoadKg: 72.5 },
  "set variables are trimmed and parsed",
);
check.equal(plain(loadConfig({ KILN_PORT: "0" })).port, 0, "KILN_PORT may be 0, meaning any free port");
check.equal(plain(loadConfig({ KILN_PORT: "65535" })).port, 65535, "KILN_PORT may be 65535");
check.equal(plain(loadConfig({ KILN_MAX_LOAD_KG: "500" })).maxLoadKg, 500, "KILN_MAX_LOAD_KG may be 500");
check.equal(
  plain(loadConfig({ KILN_PORT: undefined, UNRELATED: "x" })),
  { host: "127.0.0.1", port: 8080, maxLoadKg: 60 },
  "variables that are not set, and unrelated ones, leave the defaults",
);
check.true(Object.isFrozen(loadConfig({})), "the configuration object is frozen");

for (const bad of ["", "eighty", "1e3", "80.5", "-1", "65536", "8 080"]) {
  check.equal(
    variablesIn(problemsOf({ KILN_PORT: bad }, `KILN_PORT="${bad}"`)),
    ["KILN_PORT"],
    `KILN_PORT="${bad}" is reported as one problem naming the variable`,
  );
}
for (const bad of ["", "0", "-5", "abc", "500.5", "1e2", "12kg"]) {
  check.equal(
    variablesIn(problemsOf({ KILN_MAX_LOAD_KG: bad }, `KILN_MAX_LOAD_KG="${bad}"`)),
    ["KILN_MAX_LOAD_KG"],
    `KILN_MAX_LOAD_KG="${bad}" is reported as one problem naming the variable`,
  );
}
check.equal(
  variablesIn(problemsOf({ KILN_HOST: "   " }, "a blank KILN_HOST")),
  ["KILN_HOST"],
  "a blank KILN_HOST is reported",
);
check.equal(
  variablesIn(problemsOf({ KILN_MAX_LOAD_KG: "lots", KILN_PORT: "http", KILN_HOST: "" }, "three bad variables")),
  ["KILN_HOST", "KILN_PORT", "KILN_MAX_LOAD_KG"],
  "every problem is reported at once, in the order host, port, load",
);
check.true(new ConfigError(["KILN_PORT x"]) instanceof Error, "ConfigError is an Error");

// Type checks only: this function is compiled, never called.
export function typesOnly(config: Config): void {
  // @ts-expect-error the configuration is read-only
  config.port = 1;
}
```

**Test 3: Validates booking bodies field by field, with exact types** (hidden)

```typescript
import { validateBooking, type Cone, type ValidationResult } from "./solution.js";

const good = { member: "Ines", pieces: 6, weightKg: 12.5, cone: "6" };

function fieldsOf(body: unknown, what: string): string[] {
  const result = validateBooking(body);
  if (result.ok) fail(`validateBooking refuses ${what}`);
  return result.problems.map((problem) => problem.field);
}

const accepted = validateBooking({ ...good, member: "\tIrena Novak  " });
check.equal(
  accepted,
  { ok: true, booking: { member: "Irena Novak", pieces: 6, weightKg: 12.5, cone: "6" } },
  "a valid body is accepted with the member's name trimmed",
);

for (const body of [null, undefined, [good], "Ines", 42]) {
  check.equal(fieldsOf(body, `the body ${JSON.stringify(body)}`), ["body"], "a body that is not a JSON object is one problem on \"body\"");
}

check.equal(fieldsOf({}, "an empty object"), ["member", "pieces", "weightKg", "cone"], "an empty object misses all four fields, in order");

const badMembers: unknown[] = ["", "   ", "x".repeat(41), 7, null];
for (const member of badMembers) {
  check.equal(fieldsOf({ ...good, member }, `member ${JSON.stringify(member)}`), ["member"], "member must be a name of 1 to 40 characters");
}
check.equal(validateBooking({ ...good, member: "x".repeat(40) }).ok, true, "a member name of exactly 40 characters is allowed");

const badPieces: unknown[] = [0, 21, 2.5, "6", Number.NaN];
for (const pieces of badPieces) {
  check.equal(fieldsOf({ ...good, pieces }, `pieces ${String(pieces)}`), ["pieces"], "pieces must be a whole number from 1 to 20");
}
check.equal(validateBooking({ ...good, pieces: 1 }).ok && validateBooking({ ...good, pieces: 20 }).ok, true, "1 and 20 pieces are allowed");

const badWeights: unknown[] = [0, -1, 25.5, "12", Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY, Number.NaN];
for (const weightKg of badWeights) {
  check.equal(fieldsOf({ ...good, weightKg }, `weightKg ${String(weightKg)}`), ["weightKg"], "weightKg must be above 0 and at most 25");
}
check.equal(validateBooking({ ...good, weightKg: 25 }).ok && validateBooking({ ...good, weightKg: 0.25 }).ok, true, "25 kg and 0.25 kg are allowed");

const badCones: unknown[] = ["5", "6 ", 6, "Cone 6", "006", null];
for (const cone of badCones) {
  check.equal(fieldsOf({ ...good, cone }, `cone ${JSON.stringify(cone)}`), ["cone"], "cone must be exactly one of the four cone strings");
}
for (const cone of ["06", "04", "6", "10"]) {
  check.equal(validateBooking({ ...good, cone }).ok, true, `cone "${cone}" is allowed`);
}

check.equal(
  fieldsOf({ glaze: "celadon", ...good, pieces: 99, paid: true }, "unknown fields"),
  ["pieces", "glaze", "paid"],
  "unknown fields are problems too, after the known fields, in the order they appear",
);

// Type checks only: this function is compiled, never called.
export function typesOnly(result: ValidationResult): Cone {
  // @ts-expect-error "5" is not a cone
  const wrong: Cone = "5";
  // @ts-expect-error the booking is only there once ok has been checked
  const unchecked = result.booking;
  void wrong;
  void unchecked;
  if (!result.ok) {
    // @ts-expect-error a failed result has no booking
    return result.booking.cone;
  }
  return result.booking.cone;
}
```

**Test 4: Routes every request and answers with structured errors** (hidden)

```typescript
import { createHandler, errorResponse, loadConfig, type ApiResponse, type ErrorCode } from "./solution.js";

interface ErrorBody {
  error: { code: string; message: string; details?: unknown };
}

function codeOf(response: ApiResponse): string {
  return (response.body as ErrorBody).error.code;
}

check.equal(
  errorResponse(404, "not_found", "nothing at /kilns"),
  { status: 404, body: { error: { code: "not_found", message: "nothing at /kilns" } } },
  "errorResponse without details has no details property",
);
check.equal(
  errorResponse(400, "invalid_body", "bad", [{ field: "cone", problem: "unknown cone" }]),
  { status: 400, body: { error: { code: "invalid_body", message: "bad", details: [{ field: "cone", problem: "unknown cone" }] } } },
  "errorResponse with details includes them",
);

const handle = createHandler(loadConfig({ KILN_MAX_LOAD_KG: "20" }));
const post = (body: unknown): ApiResponse => handle({ method: "POST", path: "/firings", body });

for (const [method, path, status, code] of [
  ["GET", "/kilns", 404, "not_found"],
  ["GET", "/firings/", 404, "not_found"],
  ["GET", "/Firings", 404, "not_found"],
  ["GET", "/", 404, "not_found"],
  ["DELETE", "/firings", 405, "method_not_allowed"],
  ["PUT", "/firings", 405, "method_not_allowed"],
  ["POST", "/health", 405, "method_not_allowed"],
] as const) {
  const response = handle({ method, path, body: undefined });
  check.equal([response.status, codeOf(response)], [status, code], `${method} ${path} is answered with ${status}`);
}

const invalid = post({ member: "Ade", pieces: 3, weightKg: 1, cone: "6", price: 0 });
check.equal(invalid.status, 400, "a body with an unknown field is refused with 400");
const details = (invalid.body as ErrorBody).error.details as Record<string, unknown>[];
check.equal(
  details.map((detail) => [Object.keys(detail).sort(), detail["field"], typeof detail["problem"]]),
  [[["field", "problem"], "price", "string"]],
  "the details of an invalid body are the problems, as { field, problem } objects",
);
check.equal(codeOf(post("not an object")), "invalid_body", "a body that is not an object is invalid_body");

check.equal(post({ member: "Ade", pieces: 3, weightKg: 12.5, cone: "6" }).status, 201, "12.5 kg fits in a 20 kg kiln");
const tooMuch = post({ member: "Bo", pieces: 3, weightKg: 7.75, cone: "04" });
check.equal([tooMuch.status, codeOf(tooMuch)], [409, "kiln_full"], "7.75 kg more would be 20.25 kg, over capacity");
const exact = post({ member: "Bo", pieces: 3, weightKg: 7.5, cone: "04" });
check.equal(exact.status, 201, "a booking that fills the kiln exactly is accepted");
check.equal(
  (exact.body as { booking: { id: string } }).booking.id,
  "B-2",
  "refused bookings do not use up an id",
);
const nothingLeft = post({ member: "Cy", pieces: 1, weightKg: 0.25, cone: "10" });
check.equal(codeOf(nothingLeft), "kiln_full", "a full kiln refuses even the smallest booking");

const listing = handle({ method: "GET", path: "/firings", body: { ignored: true } }).body as {
  bookings: { id: string }[];
  loadKg: number;
  capacityKg: number;
};
check.equal(
  [listing.bookings.map((booking) => booking.id), listing.loadKg, listing.capacityKg],
  [["B-1", "B-2"], 20, 20],
  "GET /firings shows only the accepted bookings and the full load",
);

const other = createHandler(loadConfig({}));
const fresh = other({ method: "GET", path: "/firings", body: undefined }).body as { bookings: unknown[]; capacityKg: number };
check.equal([fresh.bookings.length, fresh.capacityKg], [0, 60], "each handler keeps its own bookings");
check.equal(
  (other({ method: "POST", path: "/firings", body: { member: "Di", pieces: 1, weightKg: 1, cone: "6" } }).body as { booking: { id: string } }).booking.id,
  "B-1",
  "each handler numbers its own bookings from B-1",
);

// Type checks only: this function is compiled, never called.
export function typesOnly(): ErrorCode {
  // @ts-expect-error "teapot" is not an error code
  errorResponse(418, "teapot", "short and stout");
  // @ts-expect-error error codes are exact strings
  const loose: ErrorCode = "Not_Found";
  return loose;
}
```

**Test 5: Serves JSON on 127.0.0.1 and shuts down gracefully** (hidden)

```typescript
import { MAX_BODY_BYTES, loadConfig, startServer, type Handler, type RunningServer } from "./solution.js";

const config = loadConfig({ KILN_PORT: "0", KILN_MAX_LOAD_KG: "20" });

async function call(server: RunningServer, method: string, path: string, body?: string): Promise<{ status: number; type: string; text: string }> {
  const response = await fetch(server.url + path, body === undefined ? { method } : { method, body });
  return { status: response.status, type: response.headers.get("content-type") ?? "", text: await response.text() };
}

function json(text: string, what: string): unknown {
  try {
    return JSON.parse(text);
  } catch {
    return fail(`${what}: the response body is JSON`);
  }
}

function codeIn(text: string, what: string): unknown {
  return (json(text, what) as { error?: { code?: unknown } }).error?.code;
}

// 1. The real handler behind a real server on 127.0.0.1.
const server = await startServer(config);
try {
  check.true(/^http:\/\/127\.0\.0\.1:\d+$/.test(server.url), "url is http://127.0.0.1:<port>");
  check.true(!server.url.endsWith(":0"), "url names the port the server actually listens on, not 0");

  const health = await call(server, "GET", "/health");
  check.equal([health.status, json(health.text, "GET /health")], [200, { status: "ok" }], "GET /health over HTTP");
  check.true(health.type.startsWith("application/json"), "responses are sent as application/json");

  const created = await call(server, "POST", "/firings", JSON.stringify({ member: "Ines", pieces: 2, weightKg: 4, cone: "6" }));
  check.equal(
    [created.status, json(created.text, "POST /firings")],
    [201, { booking: { id: "B-1", member: "Ines", pieces: 2, weightKg: 4, cone: "6" } }],
    "POST /firings with a JSON body creates a booking",
  );

  const listed = await call(server, "GET", "/firings?week=42");
  check.equal(
    (json(listed.text, "GET /firings") as { bookings: unknown[] }).bookings.length,
    1,
    "the query string is not part of the path",
  );

  const broken = await call(server, "POST", "/firings", "{ member: Ines");
  check.equal([broken.status, codeIn(broken.text, "malformed JSON")], [400, "invalid_json"], "malformed JSON is answered with 400 invalid_json");

  const empty = await call(server, "POST", "/firings", "");
  check.equal([empty.status, codeIn(empty.text, "an empty body")], [400, "invalid_body"], "an empty body reaches the handler as undefined");

  const huge = await call(server, "POST", "/firings", "x".repeat(MAX_BODY_BYTES + 1));
  check.equal([huge.status, codeIn(huge.text, "a huge body")], [413, "payload_too_large"], "a body over MAX_BODY_BYTES is answered with 413");

  const padding = MAX_BODY_BYTES - JSON.stringify({ note: "" }).length;
  const atLimit = await call(server, "POST", "/firings", JSON.stringify({ note: "y".repeat(padding) }));
  check.equal(atLimit.status, 400, "a body of exactly MAX_BODY_BYTES bytes is still read");

  const missing = await call(server, "GET", "/kilns");
  check.equal([missing.status, codeIn(missing.text, "an unknown path")], [404, "not_found"], "unknown paths are answered with 404 over HTTP");
} finally {
  await server.close();
}

// 2. A handler that fails: a generic 500, nothing leaked, the server keeps serving.
let calls = 0;
const failing: Handler = async (request) => {
  calls += 1;
  if (request.path === "/boom") throw new Error("kiln controller password is hunter2");
  if (request.path === "/reject") return Promise.reject(new Error("hunter2 again"));
  return { status: 200, body: { path: request.path } };
};
const fragile = await startServer(config, failing);
try {
  for (const path of ["/boom", "/reject"]) {
    const crashed = await call(fragile, "GET", path);
    check.equal([crashed.status, codeIn(crashed.text, "a failing handler")], [500, "internal"], "a handler that throws or rejects gives 500 internal");
    check.true(!crashed.text.includes("hunter2"), "the 500 response does not reveal the error's message");
  }
  const after = await call(fragile, "GET", "/still-here");
  check.equal(after.status, 200, "the server keeps serving after a handler fails");
  calls = 0;
  await call(fragile, "POST", "/x", "{ nope");
  await call(fragile, "POST", "/x", "z".repeat(MAX_BODY_BYTES + 10));
  check.equal(calls, 0, "the handler is not called for malformed or oversized bodies");
} finally {
  await fragile.close();
}

// 3. Graceful shutdown: wait for the request in flight, refuse new ones, then finish promptly.
const entered = Promise.withResolvers<void>();
const release = Promise.withResolvers<void>();
const slow = await startServer(config, async (request) => {
  entered.resolve();
  await release.promise;
  return { status: 200, body: { done: request.path } };
});
const inFlight = fetch(`${slow.url}/firings`).then(
  async (response) => [response.status, await response.json()],
  () => "cut off",
);
await entered.promise;

let closed = false;
const closing = slow.close().then(() => {
  closed = true;
});
await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 50));
check.true(!closed, "close() waits for the request in flight");
await check.rejects(() => fetch(`${slow.url}/health`), "a new connection after close() is refused");

release.resolve();
const answered = await inFlight;
check.true(answered !== "cut off", "the request in flight is answered, not cut off");
check.equal(answered, [200, { done: "/firings" }], "the request in flight gets its full response");

const outcome = await Promise.race([
  closing.then(() => "closed"),
  new Promise<string>((resolve) => setTimeout(() => resolve("still open"), 1000).unref()),
]);
check.equal(outcome, "closed", "close() finishes promptly once the last request is answered, even over a keep-alive connection");
```

## Go Development

*From your first Go program to concurrent services in production.*

A full course in four levels on Go 1.27, from zero. It teaches the language the way Go is written: values, types, functions, slices, maps, structs, pointers and errors as values, then packages and modules, methods, interfaces, generics, iterators, testing, files and JSON, then goroutines, channels, select, mutexes, context and the race detector, and finally HTTP services, structured logging, databases, profiling, security and shipping. Every level ends with a mock exam and a hands-on lab that Go builds with go test and runs under the race detector in a sandbox.

### Level I · Basic: Go Foundations

Go from zero. Learn what Go is and where it is used, install it and run a first program, then variables, constants and types, numbers, strings and runes, formatted output, if and switch, for loops, functions with several results, arrays and slices, maps, structs, pointers and errors as values, and finish with a complete program that reads and checks real input.

**After this level you can**

- Install Go, start a module, and build, run, format and vet a program
- Write programs with variables, constants, the basic types, strings, if, switch and for
- Write functions with several results, and use slices, maps and structs
- Use pointers to share and change values, and handle errors as values with if err != nil
- Read input from standard input and the command line, and build a small command-line program

#### Lesson 1: What Go Is and Where It Is Used

*20 minutes.* Learn what a program, a programming language and a compiler are, where Go came from and what it was designed for, where it is used today, how to read a whole Go program line by line, and how the labs in this course check your code.

**Objectives**

- Explain what source code, a compiler and an executable are, and how compiled and interpreted languages differ
- Describe where Go came from, what it was designed for and what the Go 1 compatibility promise guarantees
- Name the kinds of software written in Go and some well-known Go projects
- Read a small Go program and say what each line does

**Outline**

1. Programs, languages and compilers
2. Where Go came from
3. What Go was designed for
4. Where Go is used
5. Reading a whole Go program
6. Statically typed: mistakes found before the program runs
7. How this course and its labs work

#### Lesson 2: Installing Go and a First Program

*30 minutes.* Install Go 1.27, start a module with go mod init, write, run and build a first program, keep it formatted with gofmt and checked with go vet, and read a compiler error by its file, line and column.

**Objectives**

- Install Go and check the installation with go version and go env
- Create a module with go mod init and explain both lines of its go.mod
- Run a program with go run, build it with go build and run the binary
- Format code with gofmt, check it with go vet, and read a compiler error by file, line and column

**Outline**

1. Installing Go
2. A module and its go.mod
3. The first program
4. go run and go build
5. Formatting with gofmt
6. Checking with go vet
7. Reading a compiler error
8. Comments, the Playground and your editor

#### Lesson 3: Variables, Constants and Basic Types

*35 minutes.* Store values in variables declared with var and :=, rely on zero values, meet Go's basic types and type inference, swap values in one assignment, declare constants and enumerations with iota, and learn how names and scope work.

**Objectives**

- Declare variables with var and with :=, and say where each form is allowed
- State the zero value of int, float64, string and bool, and name Go's basic types
- Declare typed and untyped constants and number them with iota
- Explain "declared and not used", the blank identifier, block scope and shadowing

**Outline**

1. Variables with var
2. Short declarations with :=
3. Zero values
4. Basic types and type inference
5. Assigning several variables at once
6. Unused variables and the blank identifier
7. Constants
8. Enumerations with iota
9. Names
10. Scope and shadowing

#### Lesson 4: Numbers, Operators and Conversions

*35 minutes.* Choose between Go's integer and floating-point types, predict integer division, remainders, overflow and float rounding, use the math package and Go's operators, convert between number types explicitly, and turn numbers into text and back with strconv.

**Objectives**

- Choose an integer or floating-point type and predict overflow, integer division and remainders
- Use the arithmetic, comparison and logical operators, ++ and compound assignment, and the math package
- Convert between int and float64 explicitly and explain the mismatched types error
- Convert numbers to and from strings with strconv.Itoa, Atoi, ParseFloat and FormatFloat

**Outline**

1. Integer types and overflow
2. Integer division and remainders
3. Floating-point numbers and the math package
4. Operators, precedence and compound assignment
5. Comparisons and logical operators
6. Explicit conversions
7. Numbers and text with strconv
8. Bits and untyped constants

#### Lesson 5: Strings, Bytes and Runes

*35 minutes.* Understand Go strings as immutable sequences of UTF-8 bytes, tell bytes from runes, write string literals with escapes and backquotes, and search, cut, split, join, trim, replace, compare and build text with the strings package.

**Objectives**

- Explain why len counts bytes, what indexing and slicing a string give, and what a rune is
- Write interpreted and raw string literals and use the common escape sequences
- Search, cut, split, join, trim, replace and change the case of text with the strings package
- Compare strings, with and without case, and build longer text with strings.Builder

**Outline**

1. A string is a sequence of bytes
2. UTF-8 and runes
3. String literals
4. Joining strings
5. Searching, changing case, trimming and replacing
6. Splitting, joining and cutting
7. Comparing strings
8. Building text with strings.Builder

#### Lesson 6: Formatting Output with fmt

*35 minutes.* Print values exactly the way you want with the Print, Println and Printf families, format verbs, width and precision, send text to standard output or standard error, and let go vet catch verbs that do not match their arguments.

**Objectives**

- Choose between Print, Println and Printf, and between the Print, Sprint and Fprint forms
- Format integers, floats, strings, runes and booleans with the right verb, including %v, %T and %q
- Set width, precision, padding and alignment to print an aligned table
- Read fmt's %!verb markers and go vet's printf reports, and fix the call

**Outline**

1. Print, Println and Printf
2. The general verbs: %v, %#v, %T and %%
3. Verbs for numbers, runes, text and booleans
4. Width, precision and alignment
5. Printing a table
6. Sprintf and Fprintln: where the text goes
7. When a verb does not match its argument

#### Lesson 7: Making Decisions with if and switch

*35 minutes.* Choose what a program does with if, else if and else, an if with a short statement and string comparisons, and with switch on a value, with several values per case, with no condition and with a short statement, plus default and the rare fallthrough.

**Objectives**

- Write if, else if and else chains, and read the errors for a missing brace, a misplaced else and a non-boolean condition
- Use an if or a switch with a short statement and say where its variable can be used
- Write a switch on a value with several values per case and a default, and explain why Go does not fall through
- Replace an if-else chain with a switch that has no condition, putting the cases in the right order

**Outline**

1. if, else if and else
2. Braces, conditions and the else line
3. An if with a short statement
4. Comparing strings
5. switch on a value
6. No fall-through, and the fallthrough keyword
7. switch with no condition
8. switch with a short statement

#### Lesson 8: Repeating with for

*35 minutes.* Repeat work with Go's only loop, for, in its three-part, condition-only and endless forms, steer it with break, continue and labels, and range over integers, strings (rune by rune) and a first slice, with the common sum, count, search and build patterns.

**Objectives**

- Write the three-part, condition-only and endless forms of for, and stop or skip iterations with break and continue
- Leave nested loops at once with a label and break Label or continue Label
- Range over an integer, a string (byte index and rune) and a slice literal
- Write the sum, count, search and build-a-string loop patterns, avoiding the off-by-one panic

**Outline**

1. The three-part for
2. A condition only, or no condition at all
3. continue
4. range over an integer
5. range over a string
6. A first look at range over a slice
7. Labels for nested loops
8. Each iteration has its own variable
9. Loop patterns: sum, count, search, build

#### Lesson 9: Functions

*40 minutes.* Declare functions with parameters and results, return several values (a value plus ok or plus an error), use named results, variadic parameters, function values and types, anonymous functions and closures, recursion with a base case, and a first look at defer.

**Objectives**

- Declare and call functions with parameters and one or more results, and read the errors for wrong calls and missing returns
- Return a value with an ok flag or an error, and explain why Go uses multiple results for this
- Write variadic functions, pass functions as values, and build a closure that keeps its own state
- Write a recursive function with a base case, and say when a deferred call runs

**Outline**

1. Declaring and calling a function
2. Several results
3. Named results
4. Variadic parameters
5. Functions as values
6. Anonymous functions and closures
7. Recursion
8. defer, in brief
9. No default arguments, no overloading

#### Lesson 10: Arrays and Slices

*40 minutes.* Store lists of values in fixed-length arrays and growable slices, use make, len, cap, append and copy, see how slicing shares memory, tell nil from empty slices, build 2D slices, and use the slices package to search, sort, compare and delete.

**Objectives**

- Explain why an array's length is part of its type and why assigning an array copies it
- Create slices with literals and make, grow them with append, and say what len and cap report
- Predict when two slices share elements, and avoid it with copy or a full slice expression
- Use slices.Contains, Index, Sort, Max, Min, Equal, Reverse and Delete

**Outline**

1. Arrays: a fixed number of values
2. Slices: literals, make, len and cap
3. Slicing shares the array
4. copy, nil and empty
5. range, and slices of slices
6. The slices package
7. Strings to slices

#### Lesson 11: Maps

*35 minutes.* Store values under keys with Go's built-in map type, tell a missing key from a stored zero with the comma-ok idiom, delete entries, loop in a stable order, count and group with maps, and avoid the nil-map panic.

**Objectives**

- Create maps with literals and make, and read, write, delete and count their entries
- Tell a missing key from a stored zero value with the comma-ok idiom
- Loop over a map in a stable order by sorting its keys
- Explain the nil-map panic, which types can be keys, and why a function can change a map it is given

**Outline**

1. A map is a lookup table
2. Missing keys and the comma-ok idiom
3. Deleting entries and looping in order
4. Counting and grouping
5. The nil map
6. Which types can be keys
7. Maps are shared, not copied

#### Lesson 12: Structs

*35 minutes.* Group related values into your own types with structs, build them with field names, print them with %+v, keep them in slices and maps, compare them, and see why passing a struct to a function hands over a copy.

**Objectives**

- Define a struct type, build values with keyed literals and read and set their fields
- Store structs in slices and maps and change them there correctly
- Compare structs with == and use anonymous structs for small tables
- Explain why a function cannot change the caller's struct, and write constructor functions

**Outline**

1. Defining a struct type
2. Struct literals: name the fields
3. Structs in structs, slices and maps
4. Anonymous structs and comparing structs
5. Structs are values
6. Constructor functions
7. New types from other types

#### Lesson 13: Pointers

*35 minutes.* Take a variable's address with &, follow a pointer with *, let functions change the caller's values and structs, return a pointer or nil, avoid the nil pointer panic, fill optional fields with Go 1.26's new(expr), and decide when a pointer is the right choice.

**Objectives**

- Use & and * to share a variable, and read the pointer type *T
- Write functions that change the caller's value or struct through a pointer
- Return a pointer or nil, check for nil, and recognise the nil pointer dereference panic
- Create pointers with new(T) and new(expr), and choose between a pointer and a value

**Outline**

1. Every variable has an address
2. Letting a function change your value
3. Returning a pointer, or nil
4. The nil pointer panic
5. new, and new with a value
6. Pointer or value?

#### Lesson 14: Errors as Values

*35 minutes.* Return errors as ordinary values next to a function's result, create them with errors.New and fmt.Errorf, check them with if err != nil, add context and wrap with %w, recognise sentinel errors with errors.Is, and report a fatal error from main with an exit code.

**Objectives**

- Write functions that return (T, error) and create errors with errors.New and fmt.Errorf
- Check every error with if err != nil and either handle it or return it with context
- Wrap errors with %w and recognise a sentinel error through the wrapping with errors.Is
- Write error messages in Go style and end a program with a message on standard error and exit code 1

**Outline**

1. An error is a value
2. Returning errors of your own
3. Handle it or return it
4. Wrapping with %w, and sentinel errors
5. Writing good error messages
6. Errors in main, and panics

#### Lesson 15: Reading Input and Putting It Together

*40 minutes.* Read command-line arguments with os.Args and the flag package, read standard input line by line with bufio.Scanner, report bad lines with their numbers on standard error, set exit codes, and build a complete command-line program from small functions.

**Objectives**

- Read command-line arguments with os.Args and define flags with flag.Int and flag.Parse
- Read standard input line by line with bufio.Scanner and check its error
- Report bad input lines with their line numbers on standard error and exit with the right code
- Structure a program as small, testable functions and a main that wires them together

**Outline**

1. Command-line arguments
2. Flags
3. Reading standard input line by line
4. A complete program, step by step
5. Exit codes and other ways to read

#### Practice labs

One small lab per lesson, offered at the end of the lesson and checked in the sandbox like any other lab.

| After the lesson | Practice lab | What the learner does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What Go Is and Where It Is Used | The Ice Rink Board | Run a finished Go program for the first time, read what the test says about its output line by line, change the one value that is out of date, and submit. |
| Installing Go and a First Program | Planetarium Show Banner | Add two lines to a nearly finished program, switch two broken lines back on, read what the compiler and go vet report by file, line and column, and fix the program until it prints the right banner. |
| Variables, Constants and Basic Types | Ferris Wheel Shift Board | Declare a constant and variables with var and :=, work out the day's numbers from package-level variables, swap two values in one assignment, and print a zero value. |
| Numbers, Operators and Conversions | Tile Shop Quote | Work out a tiling quote with integer and floating-point arithmetic, explicit conversions, rounding up with the math package, and numbers turned into text with strconv. |
| Strings, Bytes and Runes | Crêperie Chalkboard | Cut a typed menu entry into its parts with strings.Cut and strings.CutLast, trim it, underline the name by counting runes instead of bytes, and compare names without regard to case. |
| Formatting Output with fmt | Cheese Counter Labels | Print a weighed cut of cheese as a sticky label with Printf verbs, zero padding, widths, alignment, two decimals and a percent sign, and write the scale's log line to standard error. |
| Making Decisions with if and switch | Kayak Hire Desk | Decide a kayak hire with switch and if, matching boat names in several spellings, reading the wind with a switch that has no condition, capping the price at a day rate, and refusing a hire when the harbour is closed. |
| Repeating with for | Village Bus Timetable | Generate a day's departures with a three-part for loop, skip the driver's lunch hour with continue, count the buses, and search for the next bus at or after a given time. |
| Functions | Archery Club Scoresheet | Write functions with several results, a variadic parameter, a function passed as a value and a closure that keeps a round's running total, to score an archery club's ends. |
| Arrays and Slices | Climbing Wall Shoe Hire | Keep a climbing wall's rack of hire shoes in a slice, removing and appending pairs, list the sizes in stock from a sorted copy that leaves the rack alone, and find the busiest day in a week's array of hires. |
| Maps | Plant Swap Stall | Count cuttings in a map, hand them out with the comma-ok idiom and delete, print the stall board in a stable order, and group wishes in a map of slices. |
| Structs | Park Tennis Courts | Build bookings with a constructor function, work out prices from their fields, mark bookings paid in place in a slice, and total what each person owes in a map of structs. |
| Pointers | Thursday Bowling League | Change a bowler's record through a pointer, return a pointer into a slice or nil, store an optional handicap as a *int with new, and read it back safely when pointers may be nil. |

#### Mock exam: Go Foundations Mock Exam

*30 questions · 20 minutes · pass mark 70%.* Ten questions drawn from the level's bank, from how Go builds and runs to types, slices, maps, structs, pointers and errors.

**Question 1** · One answer · `go-basic-01`

You run `go build` on a small Go program on a Linux laptop and copy the file it writes to a
Linux server with the same kind of processor. What does the server need in order to run it?

- **✔ A. Nothing else; the executable contains the compiled program and the Go runtime**
- B. An installed Go toolchain, because the file is Go source code that `go` interprets
- C. A Go virtual machine, because `go build` writes bytecode rather than machine code
- D. The `.go` source files next to it, because the executable loads them when it starts

> **Why:** Go is **compiled ahead of time**: `go build` translates the whole program into machine code
> and links it, together with the Go runtime (the garbage collector and the scheduler), into one
> static executable. That is one of Go's design goals: copy the binary and run it. There is no
> virtual machine and no interpreter, and the source files are not needed at run time. The one
> limit is that a binary runs only on the operating system and processor it was built for.

**Question 2** · One answer · `go-basic-02`

What does this program print?

```go
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	fmt.Println("Seats:", 3*12, "left")
}
```

- **✔ A. `Seats: 36 left`**
- B. `Seats:36left`
- C. `Seats: 3*12 left`
- D. `"Seats:" 36 "left"`

> **Why:** `fmt.Println` prints the values between its parentheses with **one space between each pair**
> and then ends the line. `3*12` is an expression, worked out before `Println` receives it, so
> the second value is the number 36. The quotes only mark where a string starts and ends in the
> source code; they are not part of the text that is printed. To print values with no spaces
> between them, you would build one string yourself, or use `fmt.Print` (lesson 6).

**Question 3** · One answer · `go-basic-03`

After `go mod init example.com/tidal` with Go 1.27.3, the new `go.mod` contains:

```text
module example.com/tidal

go 1.27.3
```

What does the line `go 1.27.3` mean?

- **✔ A. The module needs at least Go 1.27.3; an older Go toolchain will not build it itself**
- B. The module may only be built with exactly Go 1.27.3, and newer versions refuse it
- C. It is a note about where the module was created, which every Go version ignores
- D. It tells `go` to download the standard library of version 1.27.3 for this module

> **Why:** The `go` line sets the **minimum** Go version the module needs. Since Go 1.21 it is a real
> requirement, not advice: a Go toolchain older than that version refuses to load the module
> (by default the older `go` command downloads and runs the newer toolchain instead). Newer
> versions build it without complaint, thanks to the Go 1 compatibility promise. The standard
> library comes with the toolchain and is never downloaded per module. `go mod init` writes the
> version of the Go that ran it.

**Question 4** · One answer · `go-basic-04`

What happens when you run `go run .` on this file?

```go
package main

import "fmt"

func main()
{
	fmt.Println("Hello")
}
```

- **✔ A. The build fails with `./main.go:6:1: syntax error: unexpected semicolon or newline before {`**
- B. It prints `Hello`; brace placement is only a matter of style
- C. It prints `Hello`, and `gofmt` would later move the brace up to the line above
- D. It compiles, but `go vet` reports that the brace is in the wrong place

> **Why:** Go ends a statement automatically at the end of a line that could end one, such as a line
> ending in `)`. So `func main()` is taken as complete, and the `{` on the next line has nothing
> to belong to: a **syntax error**, at line 6, column 1. The brace must stay on the line of
> `func main()`. `gofmt` cannot repair this either: it refuses to format a file that does not
> parse. The error message reads file:line:column, then the problem.

**Question 5** · One answer · `go-basic-05`

What does this program print?

```go
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	docks := 10
	{
		docks := 20
		fmt.Println(docks)
	}
	docks = docks + 1
	fmt.Println(docks)
}
```

- **✔ A. `20`, then `11`**
- B. `20`, then `21`
- C. `10`, then `11`
- D. Nothing: the second `:=` gives `no new variables on left side of :=`

> **Why:** The inner `docks := 20` is in a new **block**, so it declares a second, separate variable
> that **shadows** the outer one until the closing brace. Inside the block `docks` is 20; after
> it, the name means the outer variable again, which still holds 10, and `docks = docks + 1`
> makes it 11. The error `no new variables on left side of :=` appears only when `:=` repeats a
> name in the *same* block. Shadowing is silent, which is why it causes bugs: use `=` when you
> mean to change the outer variable.

**Question 6** · True or false · `go-basic-06`

True or false: in this program `count` holds whatever value happened to be left in memory
until something is assigned to it, so the line may print any number.

```go
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	var count int
	var name string
	fmt.Println(count, name == "")
}
```

- A. True
- **✔ B. False**

> **Why:** False. Go never leaves a variable uninitialised: a variable declared without a value holds
> the **zero value** of its type, which is `0` for numbers, `""` for strings and `false` for
> booleans. The program always prints `0 true`. This is a deliberate design choice, unlike C,
> where a local variable without a value can hold leftover memory; Go code relies on it, so a
> counter declared with `var count int` is ready to use.

**Question 7** · One answer · `go-basic-07`

What does this line print?

```go
fmt.Println(7/2, -7/2, 7%3, -7%3)
```

- **✔ A. `3 -3 1 -1`**
- B. `3.5 -3.5 1 -1`
- C. `3 -4 1 2`
- D. `4 -4 1 -1`

> **Why:** All four values are integers, so `/` is **integer division**: the fraction is dropped,
> truncating towards zero, so 7/2 is 3 and -7/2 is -3 (not -4, which is what languages that
> round down, such as Python, give). The remainder `%` takes the sign of the left operand, so
> -7%3 is -1, keeping `x == (x/y)*y + x%y` true. Only with a floating-point operand, as in
> `7.0/2`, does `/` give 3.5.

**Question 8** · Select all that apply · `go-basic-08`

Which of these statements about Go 1.27 are true? Choose all that apply.

- **✔ A. After `var level int8 = 127` and `level++`, `level` holds -128, and no error is reported**
- **✔ B. With `litres := 7.5` and `bottles := 3`, `litres / bottles` does not compile**
- C. With `debt := -2.7`, `int(debt)` is -3, because conversion rounds to the nearest integer
- **✔ D. `strconv.Atoi("4 2")` returns 0 and an error that says `invalid syntax`**

> **Why:** Integer **overflow** wraps around silently: 127 + 1 in an `int8` becomes -128, with no panic.
> Go never converts between number types by itself, so a `float64` divided by an `int` is the
> compile error `mismatched types float64 and int`; write `litres / float64(bottles)`.
> Converting a float to an integer **truncates towards zero**, so `int(debt)` is -2, not -3;
> use `math.Round` first if you want rounding. `strconv.Atoi` returns two values, and for text
> that is not a number they are 0 and the error
> `strconv.Atoi: parsing "4 2": invalid syntax`.

**Question 9** · One answer · `go-basic-09`

What does this program print?

```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"unicode/utf8"
)

func main() {
	city := "Málaga"
	fmt.Println(len(city), utf8.RuneCountInString(city), city[1])
}
```

- **✔ A. `7 6 195`**
- B. `6 6 á`
- C. `7 6 á`
- D. `6 6 225`

> **Why:** A Go string is a sequence of **bytes** in UTF-8. `á` takes two bytes (195 and 161), so
> `len` counts 7 bytes for 6 characters, and `utf8.RuneCountInString` counts the 6 **runes**
> (code points). Indexing a string gives one byte, a number, so `city[1]` prints 195, the first
> byte of `á`, not the letter. 225 is the rune `'á'`, which you get from `[]rune(city)[1]`.

**Question 10** · One answer · `go-basic-10`

What does this program print with Go 1.27?

```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"strings"
)

func main() {
	before, after, found := strings.CutLast("backup.2026.tar.gz", ".")
	fmt.Println(before, after, found)
}
```

- **✔ A. `backup.2026.tar gz true`**
- B. `backup 2026.tar.gz true`
- C. `gz backup.2026.tar true`
- D. `backup.2026.tar.gz  false`

> **Why:** `strings.CutLast`, new in Go 1.27, slices the string around the **last** occurrence of the
> separator and returns the text before it, the text after it, and whether it was found, which
> is what a file extension needs. `strings.Cut` does the same around the **first** occurrence,
> which would give `backup 2026.tar.gz true`. Only when the separator is missing does either
> return the whole string, an empty string and `false`.

**Question 11** · One answer · `go-basic-11`

What does this line print?

```go
fmt.Printf("[%-6s|%6.2f|%03d]\n", "Iona", 3.14159, 7)
```

- **✔ A. `[Iona  |  3.14|007]`**
- B. `[  Iona|3.14  |007]`
- C. `[Iona  |  3.14|7  ]`
- D. `[Iona|3.14|007]`

> **Why:** A number after `%` is a **minimum width**, and values are padded with spaces on the left, so
> they line up on the right. The `-` flag pads on the right instead: `%-6s` gives `Iona` and two
> spaces. `%6.2f` rounds to two decimals and right-aligns the four characters `3.14` in six.
> The `0` flag pads a number with zeros, so `%03d` gives `007`. The second option swaps the
> meaning of `-`; the last one ignores the widths, which are never ignored, only exceeded when a
> value is longer than its field.

**Question 12** · Select all that apply · `go-basic-12`

With `n := 3`, which of these lines does `go vet` report?

- **✔ A. `fmt.Printf("%d items\n", "3")`**
- **✔ B. `fmt.Println("total: %d", n)`**
- C. `fmt.Printf("%v items\n", "3")`
- D. `fmt.Printf("%.1f%% off\n", 7.5)`

> **Why:** vet's printf check compares each verb with its argument. `%d` needs an integer, and `"3"` is a
> string: `fmt.Printf format %d has arg "3" of wrong type string`. Println has no verbs at all,
> so a `%d` in its text is almost certainly a mistake: `fmt.Println call has possible Printf
> formatting directive %d`. `%v` accepts a value of any type, so the third line is fine, and in
> the fourth `%.1f` matches the float while `%%` prints a percent sign without using an
> argument. Without vet, the first line would print `%!d(string=3) items` at run time.

**Question 13** · One answer · `go-basic-13`

What does this program print?

```go
n := 2
switch {
case n > 1:
	fmt.Println("big")
	fallthrough
case n > 5:
	fmt.Println("huge")
default:
	fmt.Println("small")
}
```

- **✔ A. `big`, then `huge`**
- B. `big` only, because `n > 5` is false
- C. `big`, `huge` and `small`
- D. `big`, then `small`

> **Why:** The first true case, `n > 1`, runs. `fallthrough` then runs the **body** of the next case
> without testing its condition, so `huge` is printed even though `n > 5` is false. It moves
> only one case on: the `huge` case has no `fallthrough`, so the switch ends there and
> `default` does not run. This surprise is why `fallthrough` is rare in Go; without it, a case
> never runs on into the next.

**Question 14** · True or false · `go-basic-14`

A variable declared in an if's short statement, as `n` is in
`if n := len(name); n > 16 { ... } else { ... }`, can be used in the `else` block too, but
not after the whole if statement.

- **✔ A. True**
- B. False

> **Why:** The scope of a variable declared in the short statement is the whole if statement: its
> condition, its block and every `else if` and `else` block. After the statement ends, the name
> is gone, and using it is `undefined: n`. That is why the form is used for values needed only
> for one decision, such as `if err := save(); err != nil`.

**Question 15** · One answer · `go-basic-15`

What does this loop print?

```go
for i, r := range "añb" {
	fmt.Printf("%d:%c ", i, r)
}
```

- **✔ A. `0:a 1:ñ 3:b`**
- B. `0:a 1:ñ 2:b`
- C. `0:a 1:Ã 2:± 3:b`
- D. `1:a 2:ñ 3:b`

> **Why:** `range` over a string decodes UTF-8: each iteration gives one rune and the **byte index**
> where it starts. `ñ` takes two bytes, so `b` starts at byte 3, not 2. Counting runes (the
> second option) is what `utf8.RuneCountInString` does, not what the index means. The third
> option is what printing each byte with `s[i]` gives, which splits `ñ` into two meaningless
> characters; `range` avoids that. Indexes always start at 0.

**Question 16** · One answer · `go-basic-16`

What does this program print?

```go
for i := 1; i <= 5; i++ {
	switch i {
	case 3:
		break
	}
	fmt.Print(i, " ")
}
```

- **✔ A. `1 2 3 4 5`**
- B. `1 2`
- C. `1 2 4 5`
- D. Nothing: `break` is not allowed inside a switch

> **Why:** An unlabelled `break` ends the innermost `for`, `switch` or `select`, and here that is the
> switch. The loop carries on, so every number is printed. To leave the loop from inside the
> switch, label the loop (`loop:` before `for`) and write `break loop`. The third option
> describes `continue`, which would skip the rest of the body for 3.

**Question 17** · One answer · `go-basic-17`

What does this program print?

```go
func counter() func() int {
	n := 0
	return func() int {
		n++
		return n
	}
}

func main() {
	a := counter()
	b := counter()
	fmt.Println(a(), a(), b(), a())
}
```

- **✔ A. `1 2 1 3`**
- B. `1 2 3 4`
- C. `1 1 1 1`
- D. `0 1 0 2`

> **Why:** The function that `counter` returns is a **closure**: it keeps the variable `n` it uses alive
> after `counter` has returned. Each call of `counter` creates a new `n`, so `a` and `b` count
> separately: `a` gives 1 and 2, `b` starts at 1, and `a` goes on to 3. `n` is not reset by
> calling `a` (that would be `1 1 1 1`), and it is incremented before it is returned, so the
> first call gives 1.

**Question 18** · Select all that apply · `go-basic-18`

Which of these statements about Go functions are true?

- **✔ A. A function can return several values, such as a result and an error**
- **✔ B. A function can be passed as an argument to another function**
- C. Two functions in one package may share a name if their parameter lists differ
- D. A parameter can have a default value, as in `func fare(adults int = 1) int`

> **Why:** Multiple results are ordinary in Go: `strconv.Atoi` returns a number and an error, and many
> functions return a value and an `ok` flag. Functions are values with types such as
> `func(int) int`, so they can be stored and passed. Go has **no overloading**: a second
> function with the same name is `fare redeclared in this block`, whatever its parameters. And
> it has **no default arguments**: `func fare(adults int = 1)` is a syntax error. Both keep
> every call explicit about what it runs and with which values.

**Question 19** · One answer · `go-basic-19`

What does this program print?

```go
a := []int{1, 2, 3, 4}
b := a[:2]
b = append(b, 99)
fmt.Println(a, b)
```

- **✔ A. `[1 2 99 4] [1 2 99]`**
- B. `[1 2 3 4] [1 2 99]`
- C. `[1 2 3 4 99] [1 2 99]`
- D. `[1 2 99 3 4] [1 2 99]`

> **Why:** Slicing copies nothing: `b` is a view of the first two elements of `a`'s backing array, with
> length 2 but capacity 4. Because there is spare capacity, `append` writes 99 into that same
> array, at index 2, which is `a[2]`. So `a` changes too. Only when the capacity runs out does
> `append` allocate a new array. To keep `a` safe, copy first or limit the capacity with
> `a[:2:2]`, which makes the append copy.

**Question 20** · One answer · `go-basic-20`

What does this program print?

```go
names := make([]string, 3)
names = append(names, "Ada", "Bo")
fmt.Println(len(names), names[0] == "")
```

- **✔ A. `5 true`**
- B. `2 false`
- C. `3 false`
- D. `5 false`

> **Why:** `make([]string, 3)` makes a slice of **length** 3: three empty strings, not room for three.
> `append` always adds after the last element, so `"Ada"` and `"Bo"` become elements 3 and 4,
> the length is 5, and `names[0]` is still `""`. To start empty with room for three, write
> `make([]string, 0, 3)`: length 0, capacity 3. Then the appends would give a length of 2.

**Question 21** · One answer · `go-basic-21`

What does this program print?

```go
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	stock := map[string]int{"leeks": 2}
	stock["kale"]--
	n, ok := stock["kale"]
	fmt.Println(n, ok, len(stock))
}
```

- **✔ A. `-1 true 2`**
- B. `0 false 1`
- C. `-1 false 1`
- D. It stops with a panic, because there is no key `"kale"` to decrease

> **Why:** Reading a missing key is not an error in Go: it gives the zero value of the value type, here
> 0. So `stock["kale"]--` reads 0, subtracts one and **stores** -1 under the new key `"kale"`.
> After that the key exists, so the comma-ok form gives `-1 true`, and the map has two entries.
> The tempting answer `0 false 1` assumes that changing a missing key does nothing; in fact it
> creates the key. To change only keys that exist, check with `n, ok := stock[name]` first.

**Question 22** · Select all that apply · `go-basic-22`

A function declares `var m map[string]int` and never assigns anything else to `m`. Which of
these statements are true?

- **✔ A. `len(m)` is 0**
- **✔ B. `m["a"]` gives 0**
- **✔ C. `m["a"] = 1` panics with `assignment to entry in nil map`**
- D. `delete(m, "a")` panics, because there is no map to delete from

> **Why:** `var m map[string]int` declares a map variable whose value is `nil`: no map has been
> created. A nil map behaves like an empty map for everything that only reads it: `len` is 0,
> any key reads as the zero value, `range` runs zero times, and `delete` on it does nothing.
> Only adding an entry needs storage, so `m["a"] = 1` panics with `assignment to entry in nil
> map`. Create the map with `map[string]int{}` or `make(map[string]int)` before writing to it.

**Question 23** · One answer · `go-basic-23`

What does this program print?

```go
package main

import "fmt"

type Seat struct {
	Row    int
	Booked bool
}

func main() {
	seats := []Seat{{Row: 1}, {Row: 2}}
	for _, s := range seats {
		s.Booked = true
	}
	fmt.Println(seats[0].Booked, seats[1].Booked)
}
```

- **✔ A. `false false`**
- B. `true true`
- C. `false true`
- D. Nothing: it fails to compile with `declared and not used: s`

> **Why:** Structs are values. In `for _, s := range seats`, `s` is a **copy** of each element, so
> `s.Booked = true` changes the copy, which is thrown away at the end of each iteration; the
> slice is never touched. The program compiles, because setting a field of `s` uses it. To
> change the elements themselves, index the slice: `for i := range seats { seats[i].Booked =
> true }`, or take a pointer to the element with `&seats[i]` (lesson 13).

**Question 24** · One answer · `go-basic-24`

```go
type Member struct {
	Name string
	Town string
}

members := map[string]Member{"ada": {Name: "Ada"}}
members["ada"].Town = "Frome"
```

What happens?

- **✔ A. It does not compile: `cannot assign to struct field members["ada"].Town in map`**
- B. It compiles, and Ada's town in the map becomes Frome
- C. It compiles, but changes a temporary copy, so the map still has an empty town
- D. It compiles, and panics when it runs because the key is missing

> **Why:** An element of a map is not a variable you can take the address of: the map may move its
> entries as it grows. So Go refuses to assign to a field of a struct stored in a map, at
> compile time, rather than silently changing a copy. The usual fix is to read the struct out,
> change the copy and store it back: `m := members["ada"]; m.Town = "Frome"; members["ada"] =
> m`. A map of pointers, `map[string]*Member`, is the other way round it.

**Question 25** · One answer · `go-basic-25`

What does this program print?

```go
package main

import "fmt"

func bump(n int) {
	n++
}

func bumpPointer(n *int) {
	*n++
}

func main() {
	x := 1
	bump(x)
	bumpPointer(&x)
	bumpPointer(&x)
	fmt.Println(x)
}
```

- **✔ A. `3`**
- B. `4`
- C. `1`
- D. Nothing: `*n++` does not compile, because it moves the pointer

> **Why:** `bump` receives a copy of `x`, so its `n++` changes only the copy: `x` stays 1. Each call of
> `bumpPointer(&x)` receives the address of `x`, and `*n++` increases the variable that `n`
> points to (it means `(*n)++`), so `x` becomes 2 and then 3. Go has no pointer arithmetic, so
> `*n++` can never mean "move the pointer"; `n++` on a pointer would not compile at all.

**Question 26** · One answer · `go-basic-26`

`type Entry struct { Name string; Handicap *int }` uses a nil `Handicap` to mean "no handicap
yet". In Go 1.27, which literal sets Ada's handicap to 12 in one expression?

- **✔ A. `Entry{Name: "Ada", Handicap: new(12)}`**
- B. `Entry{Name: "Ada", Handicap: &12}`
- C. `Entry{Name: "Ada", Handicap: new(int, 12)}`
- D. `Entry{Name: "Ada", Handicap: 12}`

> **Why:** Since Go 1.26, `new` accepts an expression as well as a type: `new(12)` creates a new `int`
> variable holding 12 and returns a `*int` to it (an untyped constant gets its default type).
> `&12` does not compile, because a constant has no address (`cannot take address of 12
> (untyped int constant)`); before Go 1.26 you needed a temporary variable, `h := 12` and then
> `&h`. `new` takes one argument only, and a plain `12` is an `int`, not a `*int`.

**Question 27** · One answer · `go-basic-27`

What does this program print?

```go
package main

import (
	"errors"
	"fmt"
)

var ErrFull = errors.New("minibus full")

func main() {
	a := fmt.Errorf("trip 3: %w", ErrFull)
	b := fmt.Errorf("trip 3: %v", ErrFull)
	fmt.Println(a.Error() == b.Error(), errors.Is(a, ErrFull), errors.Is(b, ErrFull), a == ErrFull)
}
```

- **✔ A. `true true false false`**
- B. `true true true false`
- C. `false true false false`
- D. `true true false true`

> **Why:** Both errors have the same text, `trip 3: minibus full`, so the first value is `true`. The
> difference is inside: `%w` **wraps** `ErrFull`, keeping it in the new error, so `errors.Is(a,
> ErrFull)` finds it. `%v` only copies the text, so `errors.Is(b, ErrFull)` is `false`. And `a`
> is a new error value, not `ErrFull` itself, so `a == ErrFull` is `false`: once an error may
> be wrapped, compare with `errors.Is`, never with `==`.

**Question 28** · Select all that apply · `go-basic-28`

Which of these error messages follow Go's conventions for error strings?

- **✔ A. `booking "x": strconv.Atoi: parsing "x": invalid syntax`**
- **✔ B. `bib 88: no runner has this bib`**
- C. `Error: Could not book the seats.`
- D. `Failed to parse seats!`

> **Why:** Go error strings are usually printed inside a longer message, as a chain of contexts joined
> by colons, so they start in lower case (unless they begin with a name), have no full stop or
> exclamation mark at the end, put the context first and include the values involved. The first
> two do exactly that. `Error: Could not book the seats.` repeats "Error", is capitalised, ends
> with a full stop and says neither which booking nor why. `Failed to parse seats!` is
> capitalised, shouts, and does not say which text failed.

**Question 29** · True or false · `go-basic-29`

A program reads standard input with a `bufio.Scanner`:

```go
scanner := bufio.NewScanner(os.Stdin)
for scanner.Scan() {
	fmt.Println(scanner.Text())
}
err := scanner.Err()
```

When the loop ends because all the input has been read normally, `err` is `io.EOF`.

- A. True
- **✔ B. False**

> **Why:** False: at a normal end of input, `Err()` returns `nil`. `Scan` returns a plain `bool`, which
> is `false` both when the input ends and when reading fails, for example on a line longer
> than the scanner's 64 KiB limit. `Err()` tells the two apart: `nil` means the input simply
> ended (the scanner does not report io.EOF as an error), and anything else is the real
> problem, such as `bufio.Scanner: token too long`. That is why a scanner loop is followed by
> `if err := scanner.Err(); err != nil { ... }`, and why a check for `io.EOF` there would never
> match.

**Question 30** · One answer · `go-basic-30`

```go
minimum := flag.Int("min", 0, "smallest number to count")
verbose := flag.Bool("v", false, "print every line")
flag.Parse()
fmt.Println(*minimum, *verbose, flag.Args())
```

The program is built as `tally` and run as `./tally -min 5 a.txt -v`. What does it print?

- **✔ A. `5 false [a.txt -v]`**
- B. `5 true [a.txt]`
- C. `0 false [-min 5 a.txt -v]`
- D. It prints an error about an unknown flag and exits with code 2

> **Why:** The `flag` package parses flags only up to the first argument that is not a flag. `-min 5`
> sets `minimum` to 5; `a.txt` is not a flag, so parsing stops there, and `-v` is left in
> `flag.Args()` as an ordinary argument, with `verbose` still `false`. Put flags before the
> other arguments: `./tally -min 5 -v a.txt` prints `5 true [a.txt]`. `os.Args[1:]` would hold
> all four words whatever the flags are.

#### Lab: Night Market Takings

*Go · about 55 minutes · 5 s per test.* Read a night market's sales sheet from standard input, validate every line into a struct with wrapped sentinel errors, total each stall in a map of structs, and print a sorted fee report, with a flag, messages on standard error and exit codes.

**Scenario**

Every Friday evening, stalls line Canal Street for the night market: dumplings, crêpes, bao,
churros. Each stall keeps a sheet of its sales, one line per sale: the stall, the amount, and
whether the customer paid in cash or by card. At midnight the organiser types all the sheets into
one file:

```text
# Canal Street night market, Friday
dumplings 4.50 cash
Dumplings 12.00 card
crepes 3.20 Cash
```

The market keeps a small fee, a percentage of each stall's takings. Until now the organiser worked
it out with a spreadsheet. It counted `Dumplings` and `dumplings` as two stalls, read a tired
stallholder's `3,20` as three hundred and twenty, and quietly skipped any line it could not make
sense of, so the fees it produced were argued about every week.

You are writing its replacement: a small command-line program that reads the file from standard
input, checks every line, prints the night's table with each stall's fee, and reports exactly
which lines need fixing, so that the organiser can correct them and run it again.

**Instructions**

Write `solution.go`. The starter declares the two types, the two sentinel errors, the row format
and every function the tests use, with their exact names, parameters and results: keep them. You
may add functions of your own. The tests call your functions directly, and also run your file as
a program, typing a sales sheet into its standard input.

1. **`parseCents(text string) (int, error)`** reads an amount of money as a whole number of cents:
   one to six digits, then, optionally, a point and exactly two more digits. `"4.50"` gives 450,
   `"12"` gives 1200, `"0.05"` gives 5 and `"007.00"` gives 700. For anything else, and for an
   amount of zero, return 0 and `ErrAmount` wrapped with `%w` as `amount "4.5": not a valid
   amount`, with the text quoted by `%q`. That rejects `"4.5"`, `"4."`, `".50"`, `"4.500"`,
   `"3,20"`, `"-4.00"`, `"+4.00"`, `"0.00"`, `"1234567"` and `""`. Check the characters yourself
   with a loop: `strconv.Atoi` alone accepts a sign such as `+4`. (`strings.Cut` splits at the
   point.)
2. **`parseSale(line string) (Sale, error)`** reads one line of the sheet: a stall, an amount and
   a payment method, separated by spaces (`strings.Fields`). Check in this order, and for the first
   problem return an empty `Sale` and:
   - not exactly 3 fields: `expected 3 fields, found 2` (with the real count);
   - a bad amount: `parseCents`'s error, as it is;
   - a method that is not `cash` or `card`, in any mix of upper and lower case: `ErrMethod`
     wrapped as `payment "paypal": unknown payment method`, with the field quoted as written.

   Otherwise return the sale, with the stall's name in lower case (so `Dumplings` and `dumplings`
   are one stall) and `Card` set to `true` for a card payment.
3. **`tally(sales []Sale) map[string]Takings`** adds up each stall's sales: how many there were,
   and the cents paid in cash and by card. A struct stored in a map cannot be changed in place
   (lesson 12): read it, change it, store it back.
4. **`formatCents(cents int) string`** writes cents as units, a point and two digits: 450 is
   `"4.50"`, 5 is `"0.05"`, 0 is `"0.00"` and 123456 is `"1234.56"`.
5. **`report(totals map[string]Takings, feePercent int) []string`** returns the table. Every line
   is `fmt.Sprintf(rowFormat, ...)` with six strings:
   - first a header: `"stall"`, `"sales"`, `"cash"`, `"card"`, `"total"`, `"fee"`;
   - then one row per stall, in alphabetical order of the names: the name, the number of sales
     (`strconv.Itoa`), then the cash, the card, the total (cash plus card) and the fee, each
     written with `formatCents`. A stall's fee is `feePercent` percent of its total, rounded
     down to the cent: `total * feePercent / 100`;
   - last a row named `TOTAL` with the sum of every column. Its fee is the sum of the stalls'
     fees, which can be a cent or two less than the fee on the grand total.

   With no stalls at all, the header is followed directly by a `TOTAL` row of zeros.
6. **`main`**:
   - Defines an int flag **`-fee`**, the percentage, with the default 10, and parses the flags.
     If the fee is not from 0 to 50, print `night market: -fee must be from 0 to 50` to standard
     error and exit with code 2. If any argument is left after the flags, print
     `night market: unexpected argument "notes.txt"` (the first one, quoted) and exit with code 2.
     Both happen before any input is read.
   - Reads standard input line by line with a `bufio.Scanner`, numbering the lines from 1. Every
     line counts, including those it skips. Remove spaces around each line, and skip it if it is
     then empty or starts with `#`.
   - Calls `parseSale` for every other line. For an error, print `line N: <the error>` to
     standard error and go on with the next line.
   - Checks `scanner.Err()` after the loop (print it to standard error and exit with code 1).
   - Prints the `report` of the valid sales with the chosen fee to standard output, one line
     each, or `no sales` when there are none.
   - If any lines were rejected, prints `1 line rejected` or `3 lines rejected` (with the real
     number) to standard error and exits with code 1. Otherwise it exits with code 0.

The sample sheet, typed into the program without flags, so the fee is 10%:

```text
# Canal Street night market, Friday
dumplings 4.50 cash
Dumplings 12.00 card
crepes 3.20 Cash
crepes 3.20 card
bao 6.75 card
crepes 3,20 cash
churros 2.50
dumplings 4.50 cash
bao 6.75 paypal
crepes 0.80 card
```

Standard output:

```text
stall      sales      cash      card     total      fee
bao            1      0.00      6.75      6.75     0.67
crepes         3      3.20      4.00      7.20     0.72
dumplings      3      9.00     12.00     21.00     2.10
TOTAL          7     12.20     22.75     34.95     3.49
```

Standard error, with exit code 1:

```text
line 7: amount "3,20": not a valid amount
line 8: expected 3 fields, found 2
line 10: payment "paypal": unknown payment method
3 lines rejected
```

Bao's fee is 10% of 6.75, which is 0.675, rounded down to 0.67.

**Tips.** Write and check the small functions first: `formatCents`, `parseCents`, `parseSale`.
`slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(totals))` gives the stall names in alphabetical order (lesson 11). Keep
`main` short: it reads, calls your functions and prints.

**Boilerplate given to the learner** (`starter.go`)

**Test 1: Reports the sample night from the instructions** (visible)

```go
import "strings"

// The sample sheet from the instructions, run as a program with the default fee.
func Test(t *testing.T) {
	sheet := strings.Join([]string{
		"# Canal Street night market, Friday",
		"dumplings 4.50 cash",
		"Dumplings 12.00 card",
		"crepes 3.20 Cash",
		"crepes 3.20 card",
		"bao 6.75 card",
		"crepes 3,20 cash",
		"churros 2.50",
		"dumplings 4.50 cash",
		"bao 6.75 paypal",
		"crepes 0.80 card",
	}, "\n") + "\n"

	ran := check.RunScript(sheet)
	check.Equal(ran.Out, strings.Join([]string{
		"stall      sales      cash      card     total      fee",
		"bao            1      0.00      6.75      6.75     0.67",
		"crepes         3      3.20      4.00      7.20     0.72",
		"dumplings      3      9.00     12.00     21.00     2.10",
		"TOTAL          7     12.20     22.75     34.95     3.49",
	}, "\n")+"\n", "the report printed on standard output for the sample sheet")
	check.Equal(ran.Err, strings.Join([]string{
		`line 7: amount "3,20": not a valid amount`,
		"line 8: expected 3 fields, found 2",
		`line 10: payment "paypal": unknown payment method`,
		"3 lines rejected",
	}, "\n")+"\n", "the rejected lines and their count on standard error")
	check.Equal(ran.Code, 1, "the exit code when some lines were rejected")
}
```

**Test 2: Reads and writes amounts of money exactly** (hidden)

```go
import "errors"

func Test(t *testing.T) {
	good := map[string]int{
		"4.50": 450, "12": 1200, "0.05": 5, "007.00": 700, "1": 100,
		"0.10": 10, "999999.99": 99999999, "250": 25000,
	}
	for text, want := range good {
		cents, err := parseCents(text)
		check.NoError(err, "parseCents of a valid amount returns no error")
		check.Equal(cents, want, "the cents parseCents reads from a valid amount")
	}

	bad := []string{
		"4.5", "4.", ".50", "4.500", "3,20", "-4.00", "+4.00", "+4", "0.00", "0", "000",
		"1234567", "1234567.00", "", ".", "4.5a", "1e3", "4..50", "4.-5", "£4.50", "4.5O",
	}
	for _, text := range bad {
		cents, err := parseCents(text)
		check.True(errors.Is(err, ErrAmount), "parseCents rejects a malformed or zero amount with ErrAmount")
		check.Equal(cents, 0, "parseCents returns 0 cents with an error")
	}

	_, err := parseCents("4.5")
	check.Equal(err.Error(), `amount "4.5": not a valid amount`, `the error message for "4.5"`)
	_, err = parseCents("")
	check.Equal(err.Error(), `amount "": not a valid amount`, "the error message for an empty amount")
	check.True(err != ErrAmount, "ErrAmount is wrapped with the amount, not returned as it is")

	cents := map[int]string{
		450: "4.50", 5: "0.05", 0: "0.00", 123456: "1234.56", 100: "1.00", 99: "0.99",
		10: "0.10", 1000000: "10000.00",
	}
	for n, want := range cents {
		check.Equal(formatCents(n), want, "formatCents writes units, a point and two digits")
	}
}
```

**Test 3: Reads sale lines and explains every rejected one** (hidden)

```go
import "errors"

func Test(t *testing.T) {
	sale, err := parseSale("dumplings 4.50 cash")
	check.NoError(err, "parseSale of a valid cash sale returns no error")
	check.Equal(sale, Sale{Stall: "dumplings", Cents: 450}, "parseSale of a valid cash sale")

	sale, err = parseSale("  Bao   6.75 \t CARD ")
	check.NoError(err, "parseSale accepts extra spaces, tabs and a method in capitals")
	check.Equal(sale, Sale{Stall: "bao", Cents: 675, Card: true}, "parseSale lower-cases the stall and reads a card sale")

	sale, err = parseSale("CrEpEs 12 Cash")
	check.NoError(err, "parseSale accepts a whole amount and a method in mixed case")
	check.Equal(sale, Sale{Stall: "crepes", Cents: 1200}, "parseSale with a whole amount")

	fieldCounts := map[string]string{
		"churros 2.50":        "expected 3 fields, found 2",
		"churros":             "expected 3 fields, found 1",
		"":                    "expected 3 fields, found 0",
		"hot dogs 3.00 cash":  "expected 3 fields, found 4",
		"bao 6.75 card extra": "expected 3 fields, found 4",
	}
	for line, want := range fieldCounts {
		sale, err := parseSale(line)
		check.Error(err, "parseSale rejects a line without exactly three fields")
		check.Equal(err.Error(), want, "the error for a line without exactly three fields")
		check.Equal(sale, Sale{}, "parseSale returns an empty Sale with an error")
	}

	sale, err = parseSale("bao 6,75 card")
	check.True(errors.Is(err, ErrAmount), "a bad amount gives an error wrapping ErrAmount")
	check.Equal(err.Error(), `amount "6,75": not a valid amount`, "the error for a bad amount is parseCents's error")
	check.Equal(sale, Sale{}, "parseSale returns an empty Sale for a bad amount")

	sale, err = parseSale("bao 6.75 PayPal")
	check.True(errors.Is(err, ErrMethod), "an unknown payment method gives an error wrapping ErrMethod")
	check.Equal(err.Error(), `payment "PayPal": unknown payment method`, "the error quotes the method as written")
	check.True(err != ErrMethod, "ErrMethod is wrapped with the method, not returned as it is")
	check.Equal(sale, Sale{}, "parseSale returns an empty Sale for an unknown method")

	_, err = parseSale("bao 0.00 cheque")
	check.True(errors.Is(err, ErrAmount), "parseSale checks the amount before the method")
	_, err = parseSale("bao 6.75 cards")
	check.True(errors.Is(err, ErrMethod), "parseSale accepts only the words cash and card")
}
```

**Test 5: Handles flags, arguments, empty, Windows and wrong sheets as a program** (hidden)
