- D. Inside a transaction, `db.ExecContext` takes part in the transaction, because it uses the same pool as `tx`

> **Why:** Open rows hold a connection from the pool until they are closed; a deferred `Close` covers
> the early returns, such as a failed `Scan`. `Next` reports false at the end and on a
> failure alike, and only `rows.Err()` tells them apart, so without it a connection lost
> halfway looks like a short, successful result.
> 
> `sql.Open` only checks its arguments and prepares the pool; it may not connect at all. Call
> `PingContext` at start-up to find out. A transaction holds one connection, and only the
> methods of `tx` run on it: `db.ExecContext` runs on another connection, outside the
> transaction, and with a small pool it can even wait forever for the connection `tx` holds.

**Question 13** · One answer · `go-professional-13`

`go test -bench . -benchmem` prints this line:

```text
BenchmarkJoinPlus-2   	     636	   2048343 ns/op	 2942730 B/op	     998 allocs/op
```

What does it tell you?

- **✔ A. One call of the benchmarked code took about 2 ms on average and allocated 998 times, about 2.9 MB in all; the benchmark ran it 636 times with GOMAXPROCS 2**
- B. The benchmark ran twice for 636 ms each, and allocated 998 objects in total over the whole run
- C. The 636 calls together took about 2 ms and allocated 2.9 MB
- D. The function took 2 arguments and returned after 636 nanoseconds

> **Why:** The columns after the name are the number of iterations the benchmark ran, then the time,
> bytes and allocations **per operation**, that is per pass of the `for b.Loop()` body. The
> `-2` after the name is the GOMAXPROCS value the benchmark ran with. So each call of the code
> took about 2,048,343 ns (2 ms) and made 998 allocations totalling about 2.9 MB, a sign of
> something quadratic such as building a string with `+=` in a loop. The totals for the whole
> run would be 636 times larger, which is why per-operation numbers can be compared between
> benchmarks that ran a different number of times.

**Question 14** · True or false · `go-professional-14`

`go build -gcflags='-m -l' .` reports `moved to heap: r` for this function:

```go
func newReading(stall string, cents int) *reading {
	r := reading{stall, cents}
	return &r
}
```

True or false: the report means the function has a bug, because `r` is freed when
`newReading` returns and the caller gets a dangling pointer.

- A. True
- **✔ B. False**

> **Why:** False. Returning the address of a local variable is perfectly safe in Go. **Escape
> analysis** sees that `r` is still reachable after the function returns, so the compiler
> allocates it on the heap instead of the stack, and the garbage collector frees it once
> nothing points to it. `-m` is not a warning: it explains where allocations come from, which
> matters only in code that a profile shows to be hot. Writing `new(reading)` instead would
> change nothing, since that value escapes in exactly the same way.

**Question 15** · One answer · `go-professional-15`

An API checks the token in a request against the one it stored. Which comparison should it
use?

- **✔ A. `subtle.ConstantTimeCompare([]byte(got), []byte(want)) == 1`**
- B. `got == want`, because Go compares strings in constant time
- C. `bytes.Equal([]byte(got), []byte(want))`, because it compares bytes rather than characters
- D. `strings.EqualFold(got, want)`, so that the case of the token does not matter

> **Why:** `==` and `bytes.Equal` stop at the first byte that differs, so a guess with a correct
> beginning takes slightly longer to reject. Over many requests an attacker can measure that
> and recover the secret one byte at a time: a **timing attack**. `crypto/subtle`'s
> `ConstantTimeCompare` (and `hmac.Equal` for MACs) takes the same time whatever the
> contents, leaking at most the length. `EqualFold` is worse still: it ignores case, which
> makes a token easier to guess, and it is not constant time either.

**Question 16** · One answer · `go-professional-16`

What does this program print?

```go
t := template.Must(template.New("p").Parse("<p>Hello, {{.}}!</p>\n")) // html/template
t.Execute(os.Stdout, "<b>Bo</b>")
t.Execute(os.Stdout, template.HTML("<b>Bo</b>"))
```

- **✔ A. `<p>Hello, &lt;b&gt;Bo&lt;/b&gt;!</p>`, then `<p>Hello, <b>Bo</b>!</p>`**
- B. `<p>Hello, <b>Bo</b>!</p>` twice: html/template only escapes `<script>` tags
- C. `<p>Hello, Bo!</p>` twice: html/template removes the tags from data
- D. `<p>Hello, &lt;b&gt;Bo&lt;/b&gt;!</p>` twice: every value is escaped, whatever its type

> **Why:** `html/template` escapes every value for the place it lands, so a plain string with markup
> is shown as text: `&lt;b&gt;Bo&lt;/b&gt;`. It does not strip tags, and it does not look for
> dangerous ones only. The type `template.HTML` tells it "this is already safe HTML", and
> switches the escaping off for that value, so the second call writes the tags as they are.
> That is why user input must never be converted to `template.HTML`: it reopens the door to
> cross-site scripting that the package closed.

**Question 17** · One answer · `go-professional-17`

`main.go` declares `var version = "dev"` and prints it. The release script builds with:

```sh
go build -ldflags="-X main.Version=v1.2.0" -o tally .
```

What does `./tally` print?

- **✔ A. `dev`: there is no variable `main.Version`, and the linker ignores `-X` for a name that does not exist**
- B. `v1.2.0`: `-X` matches variable names without regard to case
- C. Nothing: the link fails with an error naming the missing variable
- D. Nothing: the compiler rejects the program because `version` is not a constant

> **Why:** `-X importpath.name=value` sets a package-level **string variable** at link time, and the
> name must match exactly: `main.version`, with a lower-case v. For a name that does not
> exist the linker says nothing at all, so the binary keeps its default and prints `dev`,
> a mistake that is easy to ship. Only a malformed argument such as `-X version=v1` stops the
> link (`-X flag requires argument of the form importpath.name=value`). `-X` needs a
> variable, not a constant, which is why the program declares `version` with `var`.

**Question 18** · Select all that apply · `go-professional-18`

Which of these statements about building and shipping Go programs are true? Choose all
that apply.

- **✔ A. A binary built with `CGO_ENABLED=0` does not need the system's C library, so it can run in a `scratch` or `distroless/static` image**
- **✔ B. `-ldflags="-s -w"` leaves out the symbol table and debug information, but panics still print stack traces**
- C. `//go:embed ../shared/logo.png` embeds a file from a sibling directory of the package
- D. Building for `GOOS=windows` on a Linux machine needs a Windows machine or a Windows SDK

> **Why:** With cgo off, packages such as `net` and `os/user` use their pure Go versions and the
> binary is fully static; with cgo on they may link to libc, which an empty image does not
> have. `-s -w` strips the symbol table and DWARF data, which makes the file smaller but
> hurts debuggers; Go's stack traces use separate tables that stay in the binary.
> 
> `//go:embed` patterns are relative to the package directory and may not contain `..`:
> the go command reports `invalid pattern syntax`. And cross-compiling needs nothing but the
> Go toolchain: `GOOS=windows GOARCH=amd64 go build` works from any platform, as long as no
> cgo is involved.

**Question 19** · One answer · `go-professional-19`

`go vet ./...` reports:

```text
counter.go:14:9: Value passes lock by value: example.Counter contains sync.Mutex
```

for this method:

```go
func (c Counter) Value() int {
	c.mu.Lock()
	defer c.mu.Unlock()
	return c.n
}
```

What is the right fix?

- **✔ A. Give the method a pointer receiver, `func (c *Counter) Value() int`, so it locks the counter's own mutex**
- B. Nothing: vet's copylocks check is a style warning, and the code is correct as written
- C. Replace `sync.Mutex` with `sync.RWMutex`, which may be copied
- D. Call `c.mu.Lock()` in the caller before calling `Value`

> **Why:** A value receiver gets a **copy** of the `Counter`, mutex included. Locking the copy
> protects nothing: other goroutines lock the original, so reads and writes of `n` race.
> That is why vet's **copylocks** analyzer reports any copy of a value containing a lock, and
> its reports are real bugs. A pointer receiver uses the one shared mutex; and if one method
> needs a pointer receiver, all of them should have one. An `RWMutex` must not be copied
> either, and locking in the caller only moves the problem.

**Question 20** · One answer · `go-professional-20`

A module's `go.mod` says `go 1.24`. A developer with Go 1.27 adds a call to
`strings.CutLast`, which is new in Go 1.27. `go build ./...` succeeds, but `go test ./...`
fails:

```text
./berth.go:7:25: strings.CutLast requires go1.27 or later (module is go1.24)
```

Why?

- **✔ A. Since Go 1.27, `go test` runs vet's stdversion check, which reports standard library symbols newer than the module's `go` version; users on Go 1.24 could not build this code, so raise the `go` line or avoid the function**
- B. `go test` uses the Go 1.24 toolchain named in `go.mod`, while `go build` uses Go 1.27
- C. `strings.CutLast` only works in test files, so the build check runs only in `go test`
- D. It is a bug in Go 1.27: the build and the test should behave the same

> **Why:** The compiler lets a newer toolchain use its newer standard library even when `go.mod`
> names an older version, so `go build` passes on the developer's machine. But the `go` line
> promises that the module works with Go 1.24, where `strings.CutLast` does not exist.
> `go test` runs a high-confidence subset of vet on every build, and Go 1.27 added
> **stdversion** to that subset. The fix is a decision: require Go 1.27 by raising the `go`
> line (users then need 1.27), or keep 1.24 and write the code with `strings.LastIndex`.
> The toolchain is not switched down: a `go` line is a minimum, and Go 1.27 runs both commands.

#### Lab: Harbour Moorings API

*Go · about 60 minutes · 10 s per test.* Build the HTTP service that books visitor berths in a small harbour, with configuration from flags and the environment, ServeMux routes with methods and wildcards, size-limited and validated JSON, a constant-time admin token, slog request logging, panic recovery and server timeouts, all tested with httptest.

**Scenario**

Saltwick is a small fishing harbour with a dozen pontoon berths kept for visiting yachts. In
summer the harbour office takes bookings by VHF radio, by phone and by e-mail, writes them in a
ledger, and twice this season gave the same berth to two boats on the same night. The harbour
board has agreed to a small booking service: the harbour's website and the office's laptop
will both talk to it over HTTP and JSON, it will run as one binary in a container on the
office's server, and the harbour master alone may cancel a booking. The berths, the body size
limit and the address it listens on must be settable without a rebuild, and when something
goes wrong at two in the morning the logs must say what happened without ever showing the
harbour master's token. The bookings themselves live behind a `Store` interface, already
written with an in-memory version; your part is everything between the network and that
store.

**Instructions**

Write the four tasks in `solution.go`. The starter already contains, and the tests rely on:
the `Booking` type and the `Store` interface with `newMemoryStore`, the errors `ErrNotFound`
and `ErrBerthTaken`, the helpers `writeJSON` and `writeError` (which sends
`{"error":"..."}`), the types `Config` and `bookingRequest`, the variable `version`, and a
finished `main` that wires your functions together and shuts down gracefully on a signal.
Keep those as they are; add any functions and types of your own.

## 1. Configuration

**`loadConfig(args []string, getenv func(string) (string, bool)) (Config, error)`**. `args`
are the command-line arguments without the program name, and `getenv` works like
`os.LookupEnv` (`main` passes exactly that), so the tests can give both without touching the
real process.

| Setting      | Flag        | Environment variable   | Default |
| ------------ | ----------- | ---------------------- | ------- |
| `Addr`       | `-addr`     | `MOORINGS_ADDR`        | `:8080` |
| `Berths`     | `-berths`   | `MOORINGS_BERTHS`      | `12`    |
| `MaxBody`    | `-max-body` | `MOORINGS_MAX_BODY`    | `4096`  |
| `AdminToken` | none        | `MOORINGS_ADMIN_TOKEN` | none    |

- A flag wins over the environment, which wins over the default. Use a `flag.FlagSet` with
  `flag.ContinueOnError` (and `SetOutput(io.Discard)`), and return the error of `Parse`, so an
  unknown flag such as `-admin-token` is an error: secrets never go in flags.
- An environment value that is not a number gives an error naming the variable, such as
  `MOORINGS_BERTHS: "lots" is not a number`.
- Then validate, in this order, with exactly these errors:
  `berths must be between 1 and 200`, `max-body must be between 256 and 1048576`, and
  `MOORINGS_ADMIN_TOKEN must be set to at least 16 characters`.

## 2. Routes and handlers

**`newServer(cfg Config, store Store, logger *slog.Logger) http.Handler`** registers these
routes on a new `http.ServeMux`, with Go 1.22 patterns, and returns the mux wrapped as
`logRequests(logger, recoverPanics(logger, mux))`. Every response with a body is JSON, sent
with `writeJSON` or `writeError`; requests use `r.Context()` when calling the store.

- **`GET /healthz`**: 200 and `{"status":"ok","version":"<version>"}`, from the `version`
  variable.
- **`POST /bookings`**: read the body through `http.MaxBytesReader` with `cfg.MaxBody`, and
  decode it into a `bookingRequest` with a `json.Decoder` that disallows unknown fields
  (so a request that sends its own `"id"` is refused). The body must hold exactly one JSON
  value: decode once more and expect `io.EOF`.
  - Body over the limit: **413** `request body too large` (the error is an
    `*http.MaxBytesError`: use `errors.AsType`). Any other decoding problem: **400**
    `invalid JSON body`.
  - Then check the fields in this order and answer **422** with the first problem:

    | Rule | Error |
    | ---- | ----- |
    | `boat`, with the spaces around it removed, is not empty | `boat is required` |
    | `boat` has at most 40 characters (runes, not bytes) | `boat must be at most 40 characters` |
    | `length_m` is more than 0 and at most 20 | `length_m must be more than 0 and at most 20` |
    | `berth` is from 1 to `cfg.Berths` | `berth must be between 1 and 12` (with the real number) |
    | `arrive` parses with `time.DateOnly` | `arrive must be a date like 2026-07-04` |
    | `nights` is from 1 to 14 | `nights must be between 1 and 14` |

  - Store the trimmed boat name with `store.Add`. `ErrBerthTaken` gives **409**
    `berth is taken for those nights`; any other error **500** `internal error` (log the error
    itself with `logger`, never send it to the client).
  - Success: **201**, the header `Location: /bookings/<id>`, and the stored booking as JSON.
- **`GET /bookings/{id}`**: 200 and the booking; `ErrNotFound` gives **404**
  `booking not found`; other errors 500 as above.
- **`DELETE /bookings/{id}`**: first check the header `Authorization: Bearer <token>`: the
  token after exactly `Bearer ` must equal `cfg.AdminToken`, compared with
  `subtle.ConstantTimeCompare`. Otherwise **401** `unauthorized`, before looking anything up.
  Then cancel: **204** with no body, or 404 `booking not found`.

The `ServeMux` answers 405 for a wrong method and 404 for an unknown path by itself.

## 3. Middleware

- **`logRequests(logger *slog.Logger, next http.Handler) http.Handler`** calls `next`, then
  logs one line at level Info with the message `request` and exactly the attributes `method`,
  `path` (`r.URL.Path`, so never the query) and `status` (an int). To know the status, pass
  `next` a wrapper around the `ResponseWriter` that remembers the code given to
  `WriteHeader`; a handler that only calls `Write`, or writes nothing, has status 200. Never
  log headers: they hold the token.
- **`recoverPanics(logger *slog.Logger, next http.Handler) http.Handler`** calls `next` with a
  deferred `recover`. After a panic, it logs at level Error the message `panic` with exactly
  the attributes `path` and `panic` (the panic value as text, `fmt.Sprint(v)`), and answers
  **500** `internal error`.

## 4. The server

**`newHTTPServer(cfg Config, h http.Handler) *http.Server`** returns a server with `Addr`
from `cfg`, `Handler` `h`, `ReadHeaderTimeout` 5 s, `ReadTimeout` 10 s, `WriteTimeout` 10 s
and `IdleTimeout` 60 s.

## Example

```text
loadConfig([]string{"-berths", "8"}, env with MOORINGS_ADMIN_TOKEN=pier-head-7f3a9c2e)
  -> Config{Addr: ":8080", Berths: 8, MaxBody: 4096, AdminToken: "pier-head-7f3a9c2e"}

POST /bookings   {"boat":"Sea Pie","length_m":9.5,"berth":3,"arrive":"2026-07-04","nights":2}
  -> 201, Location: /bookings/b1
     {"id":"b1","boat":"Sea Pie","length_m":9.5,"berth":3,"arrive":"2026-07-04","nights":2}
GET /bookings/b1  -> 200, the same booking
DELETE /bookings/b1 with Authorization: Bearer pier-head-7f3a9c2e  -> 204
GET /bookings/b1  -> 404 {"error":"booking not found"}
GET /healthz      -> 200 {"status":"ok","version":"dev"}
```

The log line of the `POST`, from a JSON handler with the time removed:

```json
{"level":"INFO","msg":"request","method":"POST","path":"/bookings","status":201}
```

**Tips.** Write `loadConfig` and test it on its own first. Keep the handlers small: a struct
that holds `cfg`, `store` and `logger`, with one method per route, keeps `newServer` short. The
tests use `httptest.NewRecorder` and one `httptest.NewServer` on the loopback interface.

**Boilerplate given to the learner** (`starter.go`)

```go
// Command moorings is the visitor moorings service of Saltwick harbour.
package main

import (
	"context"
	"encoding/json"
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"log/slog"
	"net/http"
	"os"
	"os/signal"
	"strconv"
	"sync"
	"syscall"
	"time"
)

// version is set at build time with -ldflags "-X main.version=...".
var version = "dev"

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Given: the bookings and their store.

// Booking is one visiting boat's stay on a berth.
type Booking struct {
	ID      string  `json:"id"`
	Boat    string  `json:"boat"`
	LengthM float64 `json:"length_m"`
	Berth   int     `json:"berth"`
	Arrive  string  `json:"arrive"` // a date such as "2026-07-04"
	Nights  int     `json:"nights"`
}

// Errors a Store returns.
var (
	ErrNotFound   = errors.New("booking not found")
	ErrBerthTaken = errors.New("berth is taken for those nights")
)

// Store keeps the bookings. The harbour runs the service with memoryStore;
// a database/sql version would satisfy the same interface.
type Store interface {
	// Add stores a new booking, gives it an ID and returns it. It returns
	// ErrBerthTaken when another booking has the berth on one of the nights.
	Add(ctx context.Context, b Booking) (Booking, error)
	// Get returns the booking with the given ID, or ErrNotFound.
	Get(ctx context.Context, id string) (Booking, error)
	// Cancel removes the booking with the given ID, or returns ErrNotFound.
	Cancel(ctx context.Context, id string) error
}

// memoryStore is a Store in memory, safe for concurrent use.
type memoryStore struct {
	mu       sync.Mutex
	last     int
	bookings map[string]Booking
}

func newMemoryStore() *memoryStore {
	return &memoryStore{bookings: map[string]Booking{}}
}

// Add stores b with the next ID: "b1", "b2" and so on.
func (s *memoryStore) Add(_ context.Context, b Booking) (Booking, error) {
	start, err := time.Parse(time.DateOnly, b.Arrive)
	if err != nil {
		return Booking{}, err
	}
	end := start.AddDate(0, 0, b.Nights)
	s.mu.Lock()
	defer s.mu.Unlock()
	for _, other := range s.bookings {
		otherStart, _ := time.Parse(time.DateOnly, other.Arrive)
		otherEnd := otherStart.AddDate(0, 0, other.Nights)
		if other.Berth == b.Berth && start.Before(otherEnd) && otherStart.Before(end) {
			return Booking{}, ErrBerthTaken
		}
	}
	s.last++
	b.ID = "b" + strconv.Itoa(s.last)
	s.bookings[b.ID] = b
	return b, nil
}

// Get returns the booking with the given ID.
func (s *memoryStore) Get(_ context.Context, id string) (Booking, error) {
	s.mu.Lock()
	defer s.mu.Unlock()
	b, ok := s.bookings[id]
	if !ok {
		return Booking{}, ErrNotFound
	}
	return b, nil
}

// Cancel removes the booking with the given ID.
func (s *memoryStore) Cancel(_ context.Context, id string) error {
	s.mu.Lock()
	defer s.mu.Unlock()
	if _, ok := s.bookings[id]; !ok {
		return ErrNotFound
	}
	delete(s.bookings, id)
	return nil
}

// writeJSON writes v as JSON with the given status code.
func writeJSON(w http.ResponseWriter, status int, v any) {
	w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
	w.WriteHeader(status)
	json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(v) // an error means the client has gone: nothing left to do
}

// writeError writes {"error": message} with the given status code.
func writeError(w http.ResponseWriter, status int, message string) {
	writeJSON(w, status, map[string]string{"error": message})
}

// Config is the service's configuration.
type Config struct {
	Addr       string // the address to listen on
	Berths     int    // visitor berths, numbered from 1
	MaxBody    int64  // the largest request body accepted, in bytes
	AdminToken string // the token that may cancel bookings
}

// bookingRequest is the body of POST /bookings. It has no ID: the store
// assigns it, so a request that sends one is refused as an unknown field.
type bookingRequest struct {
	Boat    string  `json:"boat"`
	LengthM float64 `json:"length_m"`
	Berth   int     `json:"berth"`
	Arrive  string  `json:"arrive"`
	Nights  int     `json:"nights"`
}

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Task 1: loadConfig reads the configuration from flags, then the environment,
// then the defaults. The admin token comes only from the environment.
func loadConfig(args []string, getenv func(string) (string, bool)) (Config, error) {
	panic("not implemented")
}

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Task 2: newServer returns the service's handler: the routes on a ServeMux,
// wrapped in recoverPanics and, outside that, logRequests.
func newServer(cfg Config, store Store, logger *slog.Logger) http.Handler {
	panic("not implemented")
}

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Task 3: middleware.

// logRequests logs one line per request, after it has been handled.
func logRequests(logger *slog.Logger, next http.Handler) http.Handler {
	panic("not implemented")
}

// recoverPanics turns a panic in a handler into a logged error and a 500.
func recoverPanics(logger *slog.Logger, next http.Handler) http.Handler {
	panic("not implemented")
}

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Task 4: newHTTPServer returns a server for h with timeouts.
func newHTTPServer(cfg Config, h http.Handler) *http.Server {
	panic("not implemented")
}

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Given: main wires everything together and shuts down gracefully.

func main() {
	cfg, err := loadConfig(os.Args[1:], os.LookupEnv)
	if err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "moorings:", err)
		os.Exit(2)
	}
	logger := slog.New(slog.NewJSONHandler(os.Stderr, nil))
	srv := newHTTPServer(cfg, newServer(cfg, newMemoryStore(), logger))

	ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM)
	defer stop()
	failed := make(chan error, 1)
	go func() { failed <- srv.ListenAndServe() }()
	logger.Info("listening", "addr", cfg.Addr, "version", version)

	select {
	case err := <-failed:
		logger.Error("server stopped", "err", err)
		os.Exit(1)
	case <-ctx.Done():
		logger.Info("shutting down", "cause", context.Cause(ctx))
	}
	shutdownCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 10*time.Second)
	defer cancel()
	if err := srv.Shutdown(shutdownCtx); err != nil {
		logger.Error("shutdown", "err", err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
}
```

**Test cases the backend runs**

**Test 1: Books, reads and cancels a mooring as in the instructions** (visible)

```go
import (
	"bufio"
	"bytes"
	"encoding/json"
	"io"
	"log/slog"
	"net/http"
	"net/http/httptest"
	"strings"
)

// Helpers shared by the tests.

const mooringToken = "pier-head-7f3a9c2e" // the admin token in the tests

// mooringEnv returns a lookup function like os.LookupEnv over the given
// name, value pairs.
func mooringEnv(pairs ...string) func(string) (string, bool) {
	env := map[string]string{}
	for i := 0; i+1 < len(pairs); i += 2 {
		env[pairs[i]] = pairs[i+1]
	}
	return func(name string) (string, bool) {
		v, ok := env[name]
		return v, ok
	}
}

// mooringConfig is a valid configuration with the defaults.
func mooringConfig() Config {
	return Config{Addr: ":8080", Berths: 12, MaxBody: 4096, AdminToken: mooringToken}
}

// mooringLogger logs JSON lines to buf, without the time, so they can be checked.
func mooringLogger(buf *bytes.Buffer) *slog.Logger {
	return slog.New(slog.NewJSONHandler(buf, &slog.HandlerOptions{
		ReplaceAttr: func(groups []string, a slog.Attr) slog.Attr {
			if a.Key == slog.TimeKey && len(groups) == 0 {
				return slog.Attr{}
			}
			return a
		},
	}))
}

// mooringRecords parses the JSON log lines in buf.
func mooringRecords(buf *bytes.Buffer) []map[string]any {
	var records []map[string]any
	lines := bufio.NewScanner(bytes.NewReader(buf.Bytes()))
	for lines.Scan() {
		var record map[string]any
		if err := json.Unmarshal(lines.Bytes(), &record); err != nil {
			check.Fail("every log line is one JSON object", lines.Text())
		}
		records = append(records, record)
	}
	return records
}

// mooringCall sends one request to h. headers are name, value pairs.
func mooringCall(h http.Handler, method, path, body string, headers ...string) *httptest.ResponseRecorder {
	req := httptest.NewRequest(method, path, strings.NewReader(body))
	if body != "" {
		req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
	}
	for i := 0; i+1 < len(headers); i += 2 {
		req.Header.Set(headers[i], headers[i+1])
	}
	rec := httptest.NewRecorder()
	h.ServeHTTP(rec, req)
	return rec
}

// mooringError decodes an {"error": "..."} body.
func mooringError(rec *httptest.ResponseRecorder) string {
	var body struct{ Error string }
	if err := json.Unmarshal(rec.Body.Bytes(), &body); err != nil {
		return "(not a JSON error body: " + rec.Body.String() + ")"
	}
	return body.Error
}

// mooringBody builds a booking request body, with the given fields replaced.
func mooringBody(replace map[string]any) string {
	fields := map[string]any{"boat": "Kittiwake", "length_m": 7.2, "berth": 2, "arrive": "2026-08-10", "nights": 3}
	for k, v := range replace {
		if v == nil {
			delete(fields, k)
		} else {
			fields[k] = v
		}
	}
	data, _ := json.Marshal(fields)
	return string(data)
}

func Test(t *testing.T) {
	cfg, err := loadConfig([]string{"-berths", "8"}, mooringEnv("MOORINGS_ADMIN_TOKEN", mooringToken))
	check.NoError(err, `loadConfig(["-berths", "8"], with MOORINGS_ADMIN_TOKEN set)`)
	check.Equal(cfg, Config{Addr: ":8080", Berths: 8, MaxBody: 4096, AdminToken: mooringToken},
		`the Config from loadConfig(["-berths", "8"], with MOORINGS_ADMIN_TOKEN set)`)

	var logs bytes.Buffer
	srv := httptest.NewServer(newServer(cfg, newMemoryStore(), mooringLogger(&logs)))
	defer srv.Close()
	client := srv.Client()

	resp, err := client.Post(srv.URL+"/bookings", "application/json",
		strings.NewReader(`{"boat":"Sea Pie","length_m":9.5,"berth":3,"arrive":"2026-07-04","nights":2}`))
	check.NoError(err, "POST /bookings")
	body, _ := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
	resp.Body.Close()
	check.Equal(resp.StatusCode, http.StatusCreated, "the status of POST /bookings")
	check.Equal(resp.Header.Get("Location"), "/bookings/b1", "the Location header of POST /bookings")
	check.True(strings.HasPrefix(resp.Header.Get("Content-Type"), "application/json"), "the Content-Type of POST /bookings")
	var created Booking
	check.NoError(json.Unmarshal(body, &created), "the body of POST /bookings is a JSON booking")
	check.Equal(created, Booking{ID: "b1", Boat: "Sea Pie", LengthM: 9.5, Berth: 3, Arrive: "2026-07-04", Nights: 2},
		"the booking returned by POST /bookings")

	resp, err = client.Get(srv.URL + "/bookings/b1")
	check.NoError(err, "GET /bookings/b1")
	var got Booking
	check.NoError(json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(&got), "the body of GET /bookings/b1 is a JSON booking")
	resp.Body.Close()
	check.Equal(resp.StatusCode, http.StatusOK, "the status of GET /bookings/b1")
	check.Equal(got, created, "the booking returned by GET /bookings/b1")

	req, _ := http.NewRequest(http.MethodDelete, srv.URL+"/bookings/b1", nil)
	req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+mooringToken)
	resp, err = client.Do(req)
	check.NoError(err, "DELETE /bookings/b1 with the admin token")
	resp.Body.Close()
	check.Equal(resp.StatusCode, http.StatusNoContent, "the status of DELETE /bookings/b1 with the admin token")

	h := newServer(cfg, newMemoryStore(), mooringLogger(&logs))
	missing := mooringCall(h, http.MethodGet, "/bookings/b1", "")
	check.Equal(missing.Code, http.StatusNotFound, "the status of GET for a booking that does not exist")
	check.Equal(mooringError(missing), "booking not found", "the error of GET for a booking that does not exist")
	health := mooringCall(h, http.MethodGet, "/healthz", "")
	check.Equal(health.Code, http.StatusOK, "the status of GET /healthz")
	check.Equal(strings.TrimSpace(health.Body.String()), `{"status":"ok","version":"dev"}`, "the body of GET /healthz")

	records := mooringRecords(&logs)
	check.Equal(len(records), 5, "the number of log lines for five requests")
	check.Equal(records[0], map[string]any{"level": "INFO", "msg": "request", "method": "POST", "path": "/bookings", "status": 201.0},
		"the log line of POST /bookings")
}
```

**Test 2: Loads the configuration with flags over the environment over the defaults, and validates it** (hidden)

```go
import "strings"

func Test(t *testing.T) {
	token := mooringEnv("MOORINGS_ADMIN_TOKEN", mooringToken)

	cfg, err := loadConfig(nil, token)
	check.NoError(err, "loadConfig with only the admin token set")
	check.Equal(cfg, Config{Addr: ":8080", Berths: 12, MaxBody: 4096, AdminToken: mooringToken},
		"the Config with only the admin token set: every other setting has its default")

	env := mooringEnv(
		"MOORINGS_ADDR", "127.0.0.1:9090",
		"MOORINGS_BERTHS", "30",
		"MOORINGS_MAX_BODY", "8192",
		"MOORINGS_ADMIN_TOKEN", mooringToken,
	)
	cfg, err = loadConfig(nil, env)
	check.NoError(err, "loadConfig with every setting in the environment")
	check.Equal(cfg, Config{Addr: "127.0.0.1:9090", Berths: 30, MaxBody: 8192, AdminToken: mooringToken},
		"the environment overrides the defaults")

	cfg, err = loadConfig([]string{"-addr", ":7000", "-berths=40", "-max-body", "2048"}, env)
	check.NoError(err, "loadConfig with flags and the environment")
	check.Equal(cfg, Config{Addr: ":7000", Berths: 40, MaxBody: 2048, AdminToken: mooringToken},
		"flags override the environment")

	cfg, err = loadConfig([]string{"-berths", "5"}, env)
	check.NoError(err, "loadConfig with one flag and the environment")
	check.Equal(cfg, Config{Addr: "127.0.0.1:9090", Berths: 5, MaxBody: 8192, AdminToken: mooringToken},
		"a flag overrides only its own setting")

	_, err = loadConfig([]string{"-admin-token", mooringToken}, token)
	check.Error(err, "there is no -admin-token flag: secrets never go in flags")
	_, err = loadConfig([]string{"-colour", "blue"}, token)
	check.Error(err, "loadConfig with an unknown flag")
	_, err = loadConfig([]string{"-berths", "many"}, token)
	check.Error(err, "loadConfig with a flag value that is not a number")

	_, err = loadConfig(nil, mooringEnv("MOORINGS_ADMIN_TOKEN", mooringToken, "MOORINGS_BERTHS", "lots"))
	check.Error(err, "loadConfig with MOORINGS_BERTHS that is not a number")
	check.True(strings.Contains(err.Error(), "MOORINGS_BERTHS"), "the error for a bad MOORINGS_BERTHS names the variable")
	_, err = loadConfig(nil, mooringEnv("MOORINGS_ADMIN_TOKEN", mooringToken, "MOORINGS_MAX_BODY", "4k"))
	check.Error(err, "loadConfig with MOORINGS_MAX_BODY that is not a number")
	check.True(strings.Contains(err.Error(), "MOORINGS_MAX_BODY"), "the error for a bad MOORINGS_MAX_BODY names the variable")

	for _, c := range []struct {
		args  []string
		want  string
		about string
	}{
		{[]string{"-berths", "0"}, "berths must be between 1 and 200", "0 berths"},
		{[]string{"-berths", "201"}, "berths must be between 1 and 200", "201 berths"},
		{[]string{"-max-body", "255"}, "max-body must be between 256 and 1048576", "a max-body of 255"},
		{[]string{"-max-body", "1048577"}, "max-body must be between 256 and 1048576", "a max-body of 1048577"},
	} {
		_, err := loadConfig(c.args, token)
		check.Error(err, "loadConfig refuses "+c.about)
		check.Equal(err.Error(), c.want, "the error for "+c.about)
	}
	for _, args := range [][]string{{"-berths", "1"}, {"-berths", "200"}, {"-max-body", "256"}, {"-max-body", "1048576"}} {
		_, err := loadConfig(args, token)
		check.NoError(err, "loadConfig accepts the limits of each range ("+strings.Join(args, " ")+")")
	}

	_, err = loadConfig(nil, mooringEnv())
	check.Error(err, "loadConfig without MOORINGS_ADMIN_TOKEN")
	check.Equal(err.Error(), "MOORINGS_ADMIN_TOKEN must be set to at least 16 characters", "the error without an admin token")
	_, err = loadConfig(nil, mooringEnv("MOORINGS_ADMIN_TOKEN", "short-token-15c"))
	check.Error(err, "loadConfig with an admin token of 15 characters")
	_, err = loadConfig(nil, mooringEnv("MOORINGS_ADMIN_TOKEN", "exactly-16-chars"))
	check.NoError(err, "loadConfig with an admin token of exactly 16 characters")
}
```

**Test 3: Validates bookings, limits the body size and refuses clashing berths** (hidden)

```go
import (
	"bytes"
	"encoding/json"
	"net/http"
	"strings"
)

func Test(t *testing.T) {
	cfg := mooringConfig()
	cfg.Berths = 5
	cfg.MaxBody = 512
	var logs bytes.Buffer
	h := newServer(cfg, newMemoryStore(), mooringLogger(&logs))

	ok := mooringCall(h, http.MethodPost, "/bookings", mooringBody(map[string]any{"boat": "  Kittiwake  "}))
	check.Equal(ok.Code, http.StatusCreated, "the status of a valid booking")
	var b Booking
	check.NoError(json.Unmarshal(ok.Body.Bytes(), &b), "the body of a valid booking is JSON")
	check.Equal(b.Boat, "Kittiwake", "the boat name is stored without the spaces around it")
	check.Equal(ok.Header().Get("Location"), "/bookings/"+b.ID, "the Location header names the new booking")

	// Validation, in the order of the instructions.
	for _, c := range []struct {
		replace map[string]any
		want    string
		about   string
	}{
		{map[string]any{"boat": nil}, "boat is required", "no boat field"},
		{map[string]any{"boat": "   "}, "boat is required", "a boat name of spaces only"},
		{map[string]any{"boat": strings.Repeat("é", 41)}, "boat must be at most 40 characters", "a boat name of 41 characters"},
		{map[string]any{"length_m": 0}, "length_m must be more than 0 and at most 20", "length_m 0"},
		{map[string]any{"length_m": -3}, "length_m must be more than 0 and at most 20", "length_m -3"},
		{map[string]any{"length_m": 20.01}, "length_m must be more than 0 and at most 20", "length_m 20.01"},
		{map[string]any{"berth": 0}, "berth must be between 1 and 5", "berth 0, with 5 berths configured"},
		{map[string]any{"berth": 6}, "berth must be between 1 and 5", "berth 6, with 5 berths configured"},
		{map[string]any{"arrive": "10/08/2026"}, "arrive must be a date like 2026-07-04", "arrive 10/08/2026"},
		{map[string]any{"arrive": "2026-02-30"}, "arrive must be a date like 2026-07-04", "arrive 2026-02-30"},
		{map[string]any{"arrive": nil}, "arrive must be a date like 2026-07-04", "no arrive field"},
		{map[string]any{"nights": 0}, "nights must be between 1 and 14", "nights 0"},
		{map[string]any{"nights": 15}, "nights must be between 1 and 14", "nights 15"},
		{map[string]any{"boat": "", "nights": 0}, "boat is required", "an empty boat and nights 0 together"},
		{map[string]any{"berth": 9, "length_m": 25}, "length_m must be more than 0 and at most 20", "berth 9 and length_m 25 together"},
	} {
		rec := mooringCall(h, http.MethodPost, "/bookings", mooringBody(c.replace))
		check.Equal(rec.Code, http.StatusUnprocessableEntity, "the status of a booking with "+c.about)
		check.Equal(mooringError(rec), c.want, "the error of a booking with "+c.about+" (the first rule broken, in order)")
		check.True(strings.HasPrefix(rec.Header().Get("Content-Type"), "application/json"), "errors are sent as JSON")
	}
	for _, edge := range []struct {
		replace map[string]any
		about   string
	}{
		{map[string]any{"boat": strings.Repeat("é", 40), "berth": 1, "arrive": "2026-09-01"}, "a boat name of 40 characters (80 bytes)"},
		{map[string]any{"length_m": 20, "berth": 5, "nights": 14, "arrive": "2026-10-01"}, "length_m 20, the last berth and 14 nights"},
		{map[string]any{"length_m": 0.5, "nights": 1, "arrive": "2026-11-01"}, "length_m 0.5 and 1 night"},
	} {
		rec := mooringCall(h, http.MethodPost, "/bookings", mooringBody(edge.replace))
		check.Equal(rec.Code, http.StatusCreated, "a booking at the limits of the rules is accepted: "+edge.about)
	}

	// Bodies that are not one JSON object with the booking fields.
	for _, c := range []struct{ body, about string }{
		{``, "an empty body"},
		{`{"boat":`, "a body cut off halfway"},
		{`["Kittiwake"]`, "a JSON array"},
		{`{"boat":"Kittiwake","length_m":"long","berth":2,"arrive":"2026-08-10","nights":3}`, "a string where a number belongs"},
		{mooringBody(map[string]any{"id": "b99"}), "an id sent by the client"},
		{mooringBody(map[string]any{"crew": 4}), "an unknown field"},
		{mooringBody(nil) + `{"boat":"Second"}`, "a second JSON object after the first"},
		{mooringBody(nil) + ` and more`, "text after the JSON object"},
	} {
		rec := mooringCall(h, http.MethodPost, "/bookings", c.body)
		check.Equal(rec.Code, http.StatusBadRequest, "the status of a body with "+c.about)
		check.Equal(mooringError(rec), "invalid JSON body", "the error of a body with "+c.about)
	}

	big := mooringBody(map[string]any{"boat": strings.Repeat("x", 600)})
	rec := mooringCall(h, http.MethodPost, "/bookings", big)
	check.Equal(rec.Code, http.StatusRequestEntityTooLarge, "the status of a body over MaxBody")
	check.Equal(mooringError(rec), "request body too large", "the error of a body over MaxBody")
	fits := mooringBody(map[string]any{"boat": "Fits", "arrive": "2026-12-01", "nights": 1})
	fits += strings.Repeat(" ", 512-len(fits))
	check.Equal(mooringCall(h, http.MethodPost, "/bookings", fits).Code, http.StatusCreated,
		"a body of exactly MaxBody bytes is accepted")

	// A berth that is taken on one of the nights.
	first := mooringCall(h, http.MethodPost, "/bookings", mooringBody(map[string]any{"berth": 4, "arrive": "2027-01-10", "nights": 3}))
	check.Equal(first.Code, http.StatusCreated, "booking berth 4 from 10 January for 3 nights")
	clash := mooringCall(h, http.MethodPost, "/bookings", mooringBody(map[string]any{"berth": 4, "arrive": "2027-01-12", "nights": 2}))
	check.Equal(clash.Code, http.StatusConflict, "the status of a booking that overlaps another on the same berth")
	check.Equal(mooringError(clash), "berth is taken for those nights", "the error of an overlapping booking")
	next := mooringCall(h, http.MethodPost, "/bookings", mooringBody(map[string]any{"berth": 4, "arrive": "2027-01-13", "nights": 2}))
	check.Equal(next.Code, http.StatusCreated, "a booking that starts the day the last one leaves")

	check.Equal(mooringCall(h, http.MethodPut, "/bookings", mooringBody(nil)).Code, http.StatusMethodNotAllowed,
		"PUT /bookings is not allowed")
	check.Equal(mooringCall(h, http.MethodGet, "/bookings/b404", "").Code, http.StatusNotFound,
		"GET of a booking that does not exist")
}
```

**Test 4: Lets only the admin token cancel bookings, and routes every request correctly** (hidden)

```go
import (
	"bytes"
	"encoding/json"
	"net/http"
	"strings"
)

func Test(t *testing.T) {
	cfg := mooringConfig()
	var logs bytes.Buffer
	store := newMemoryStore()
	h := newServer(cfg, store, mooringLogger(&logs))

	created := mooringCall(h, http.MethodPost, "/bookings", mooringBody(nil))
	check.Equal(created.Code, http.StatusCreated, "creating a booking to cancel")
	path := created.Header().Get("Location")

	for _, auth := range []string{
		"",
		mooringToken,
		"Bearer",
		"Bearer ",
		"bearer " + mooringToken,
		"Basic " + mooringToken,
		"Bearer " + mooringToken[:len(mooringToken)-1],
		"Bearer " + mooringToken + "x",
		"Bearer " + strings.ToUpper(mooringToken),
	} {
		rec := mooringCall(h, http.MethodDelete, path, "", "Authorization", auth)
		check.Equal(rec.Code, http.StatusUnauthorized, "DELETE without exactly \"Bearer <admin token>\" is refused")
		check.Equal(mooringError(rec), "unauthorized", "the error of an unauthorized DELETE")
	}
	still := mooringCall(h, http.MethodGet, path, "")
	check.Equal(still.Code, http.StatusOK, "a refused DELETE leaves the booking in place")

	missing := mooringCall(h, http.MethodDelete, "/bookings/b77", "", "Authorization", "Bearer "+mooringToken)
	check.Equal(missing.Code, http.StatusNotFound, "DELETE of a booking that does not exist, with the token")
	check.Equal(mooringError(missing), "booking not found", "the error of DELETE for a booking that does not exist")
	missingNoToken := mooringCall(h, http.MethodDelete, "/bookings/b77", "")
	check.Equal(missingNoToken.Code, http.StatusUnauthorized, "the token is checked before looking the booking up")

	done := mooringCall(h, http.MethodDelete, path, "", "Authorization", "Bearer "+mooringToken)
	check.Equal(done.Code, http.StatusNoContent, "DELETE with the admin token")
	check.Equal(done.Body.Len(), 0, "a 204 response has no body")
	check.Equal(mooringCall(h, http.MethodGet, path, "").Code, http.StatusNotFound, "GET after the booking was cancelled")
	check.Equal(mooringCall(h, http.MethodDelete, path, "", "Authorization", "Bearer "+mooringToken).Code,
		http.StatusNotFound, "a second DELETE of the same booking")

	// The token in the configuration is the one that counts.
	other := cfg
	other.AdminToken = "harbour-master-2027-token"
	h2 := newServer(other, store, mooringLogger(&logs))
	again := mooringCall(h2, http.MethodPost, "/bookings", mooringBody(map[string]any{"arrive": "2026-08-20"}))
	check.Equal(mooringCall(h2, http.MethodDelete, again.Header().Get("Location"), "", "Authorization", "Bearer "+mooringToken).Code,
		http.StatusUnauthorized, "DELETE with a token that is not the configured one")
	check.Equal(mooringCall(h2, http.MethodDelete, again.Header().Get("Location"), "", "Authorization", "Bearer harbour-master-2027-token").Code,
		http.StatusNoContent, "DELETE with the configured token")

	// Routes and the health check.
	t.Cleanup(func() { version = "dev" })
	version = "v2.1.0"
	health := mooringCall(h, http.MethodGet, "/healthz", "")
	var status map[string]string
	check.NoError(json.Unmarshal(health.Body.Bytes(), &status), "the body of GET /healthz is a JSON object")
	check.Equal(status, map[string]string{"status": "ok", "version": "v2.1.0"}, "GET /healthz reports the version variable")
	check.Equal(mooringCall(h, http.MethodPost, "/healthz", "").Code, http.StatusMethodNotAllowed, "POST /healthz is not allowed")
	check.Equal(mooringCall(h, http.MethodGet, "/bookings", "").Code, http.StatusMethodNotAllowed, "GET /bookings is not allowed")
	check.Equal(mooringCall(h, http.MethodGet, "/berths", "").Code, http.StatusNotFound, "a path the service does not have")

	stored := mooringCall(h, http.MethodPost, "/bookings", mooringBody(map[string]any{"arrive": "2026-09-09"}))
	var b Booking
	check.NoError(json.Unmarshal(stored.Body.Bytes(), &b), "the body of a new booking")
	got := mooringCall(h, http.MethodGet, "/bookings/"+b.ID, "")
	var fetched Booking
	check.NoError(json.Unmarshal(got.Body.Bytes(), &fetched), "the body of GET /bookings/{id}")
	check.Equal(fetched, b, "GET /bookings/{id} uses the id from the path")
}
```

**Test 5: Logs every request, recovers from panics and sets server timeouts** (hidden)

```go
import (
	"bytes"
	"context"
	"errors"
	"net/http"
	"strings"
	"time"
)

// mooringFailingStore is a Store whose Get panics and whose Add fails.
type mooringFailingStore struct{ Store }

func (mooringFailingStore) Get(context.Context, string) (Booking, error) {
	panic("berth chart missing")
}

func (mooringFailingStore) Add(context.Context, Booking) (Booking, error) {
	return Booking{}, errors.New("disk full")
}

func Test(t *testing.T) {
	// logRequests on its own, around handlers that set the status in different ways.
	var logs bytes.Buffer
	logger := mooringLogger(&logs)
	teapot := logRequests(logger, http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		w.WriteHeader(http.StatusTeapot)
	}))
	writesOnly := logRequests(logger, http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		w.Write([]byte("hello"))
	}))
	silent := logRequests(logger, http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {}))

	rec := mooringCall(teapot, http.MethodGet, "/brew?strength=4", "", "Authorization", "Bearer "+mooringToken)
	check.Equal(rec.Code, http.StatusTeapot, "logRequests passes the handler's status on to the client")
	mooringCall(writesOnly, http.MethodPost, "/hello", "")
	mooringCall(silent, http.MethodDelete, "/nothing", "")
	records := mooringRecords(&logs)
	check.Equal(len(records), 3, "logRequests logs exactly one line per request")
	check.Equal(records[0], map[string]any{"level": "INFO", "msg": "request", "method": "GET", "path": "/brew", "status": 418.0},
		"the log line for a handler that calls WriteHeader (the path without the query)")
	check.Equal(records[1]["status"], any(200.0), "the status logged for a handler that only calls Write")
	check.Equal(records[2]["status"], any(200.0), "the status logged for a handler that writes nothing")
	check.True(!strings.Contains(logs.String(), mooringToken), "the Authorization header never reaches the log")
	check.True(!strings.Contains(logs.String(), "strength"), "the query string is not logged")

	// recoverPanics on its own.
	logs.Reset()
	boom := recoverPanics(logger, http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		panic("tide table corrupt")
	}))
	rec = mooringCall(boom, http.MethodGet, "/tides", "")
	check.Equal(rec.Code, http.StatusInternalServerError, "the status after a handler panics")
	check.Equal(mooringError(rec), "internal error", "the error after a handler panics")
	records = mooringRecords(&logs)
	check.Equal(len(records), 1, "recoverPanics logs one line for a panic")
	check.Equal(records[0], map[string]any{"level": "ERROR", "msg": "panic", "path": "/tides", "panic": "tide table corrupt"},
		"the log line for a panic")
	calm := recoverPanics(logger, http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		w.WriteHeader(http.StatusAccepted)
	}))
	check.Equal(mooringCall(calm, http.MethodGet, "/", "").Code, http.StatusAccepted, "recoverPanics changes nothing when there is no panic")

	// Both, in newServer: the panic is recovered inside the request log.
	logs.Reset()
	h := newServer(mooringConfig(), mooringFailingStore{newMemoryStore()}, logger)
	rec = mooringCall(h, http.MethodGet, "/bookings/b1", "")
	check.Equal(rec.Code, http.StatusInternalServerError, "newServer answers 500 when the store panics")
	records = mooringRecords(&logs)
	check.Equal(len(records), 2, "the log lines for a request whose handler panicked")
	check.Equal(records[0]["msg"], any("panic"), "the panic is logged first, by recoverPanics")
	check.Equal(records[1], map[string]any{"level": "INFO", "msg": "request", "method": "GET", "path": "/bookings/b1", "status": 500.0},
		"then the request is logged with status 500, by logRequests outside recoverPanics")

	logs.Reset()
	rec = mooringCall(h, http.MethodPost, "/bookings", mooringBody(nil))
	check.Equal(rec.Code, http.StatusInternalServerError, "newServer answers 500 when the store fails")
	check.Equal(mooringError(rec), "internal error", "the client is not told the store's error")
	check.True(strings.Contains(logs.String(), "disk full"), "the store's error is logged")

	srv := newHTTPServer(mooringConfig(), h)
	check.Equal(srv.Addr, ":8080", "the server's address comes from the configuration")
	check.True(srv.Handler != nil, "the server has the handler")
	check.Equal(srv.ReadHeaderTimeout, 5*time.Second, "the server's ReadHeaderTimeout")
	check.Equal(srv.ReadTimeout, 10*time.Second, "the server's ReadTimeout")
	check.Equal(srv.WriteTimeout, 10*time.Second, "the server's WriteTimeout")
	check.Equal(srv.IdleTimeout, 60*time.Second, "the server's IdleTimeout")
}
```

The reference solution is [`content/tracks/go/professional/lab/solution.go`](../content/tracks/go/professional/lab/solution.go).

## Solidity Smart Contracts

*From your first contract to secure, production-grade Solidity on Ethereum.*

A full course in four levels on Solidity 0.8.38 and Foundry, for people who already program. It starts from zero on blockchains: what Ethereum, accounts, gas and the EVM are, then types, functions, errors, arrays, mappings and structs, data locations, events, modifiers and payments; then interfaces, inheritance, libraries, ERC-20 and ERC-721 tokens, ABI encoding, gas, time, testing and deployment with Foundry; then the attacks that drain real contracts and how to stop them, from reentrancy and access control to oracle manipulation, signature replay and proxy storage collisions; and finally gas optimisation, assembly, upgrades, ERC-4626 vaults, AMMs, account abstraction, governance, audits and the EVM roadmap. Every lab runs in a local EVM with Foundry, and the security labs are attacked by the tests.

### Level I · Basic: Solidity Foundations

Ethereum and Solidity from zero, for people who already program. Learn what blockchains, accounts, transactions, gas and the EVM are, set up Foundry and write and test a first contract, then types and units, functions and visibility, control flow and custom errors, arrays and strings, mappings and structs, data locations, events, modifiers and access control, and receiving and sending ether, and finish with a complete, tested contract.

**After this level you can**

- Explain accounts, transactions, gas and the EVM, and why contract bugs are costly
- Build and test contracts with Foundry, reading compiler errors, reverts and test output
- Use Solidity's types, functions, visibility, mappings, structs, arrays and data locations
- Signal failure with custom errors and require, record history with events, and restrict access with modifiers
- Receive and send ether safely with call and the pull-payment pattern

#### Lesson 1: What Ethereum and Smart Contracts Are

*25 minutes.* Learn what a blockchain is, how Ethereum works as one shared computer with accounts, transactions, gas and the EVM, why contracts are public and permanent, where they run, where Solidity comes from, and how this course's labs test your code.

**Objectives**

- Explain blocks, hashes and proof of stake, and convert between ether, gwei and wei
- Tell externally owned accounts from contract accounts, and describe what a transaction contains
- Work out a transaction's fee from its gas, base fee and priority fee
- Read a small Solidity contract, say what each line does, and explain why its bugs cost real money

**Outline**

1. Who this course is for
2. A blockchain in plain words
3. Accounts, ether and wei
4. Transactions and gas
5. The EVM and smart contracts
6. Public, permanent and holding real money
7. Where contracts run and what they are used for
8. Solidity, and why it is still 0.8
9. Reading a first contract
10. How this course and its labs work

#### Lesson 2: Foundry and a First Contract

*30 minutes.* Install Foundry, create a project with forge init, read the parts of a contract, build it into bytecode and an ABI, write and run a first test with setUp, test functions and assertEq, print with console.log, format with forge fmt, and know when Remix is enough.

**Objectives**

- Install Foundry and create a project, and say what src, test, script, lib and foundry.toml hold
- Name the parts of a contract file (licence, pragma, contract, state variable, function) and build it
- Explain what the bytecode and the ABI that forge build produces are for
- Write a test contract with setUp and test_ functions, run it with forge test, and read its result

**Outline**

1. Installing Foundry
2. A new project
3. The parts of a contract
4. Building: bytecode and the ABI
5. A first test
6. Printing with console.log
7. Formatting with forge fmt
8. Remix, in the browser

#### Lesson 3: Types, Variables and Units

*35 minutes.* Use Solidity's value types (bool, integers of every size, address, fixed-size bytes, enums), see checked arithmetic revert with panic 0x11, write amounts and durations with units, fix values with constant and immutable, and convert between types knowing what truncates.

**Objectives**

- Choose between bool, uint8 to uint256, int types, address, address payable, bytes1 to bytes32 and enums, and state each default value
- Predict when checked arithmetic reverts with panic 0x11, and widen values before adding them
- Write amounts with ether, gwei and wei and durations with time units, and declare constant and immutable values
- Convert between integer, bytes and address types, and say which conversions truncate

**Outline**

1. Value types and their defaults
2. Checked arithmetic and panic 0x11
3. unchecked, in one paragraph
4. Addresses
5. Literals and units
6. constant, immutable and ordinary state variables
7. Conversions and what truncates

#### Lesson 4: Functions and Visibility

*35 minutes.* Declare functions with parameters and named, multiple returns; choose public, external, internal or private and know that private data is still public on chain; mark functions view, pure or payable; use getters, msg.sender and the constructor; tell internal calls from external ones; and test as another account with vm.prank.

**Objectives**

- Declare functions with parameters, several and named return values, and read multiple results with destructuring
- Choose each function's visibility and explain why a private variable can still be read by anyone
- Mark functions view, pure or payable, and fix the compiler errors that the wrong choice causes
- Use msg.sender and a constructor, tell f() from this.f(), and call a contract as another account with vm.prank

**Outline**

1. Declaring a function
2. Returning several values
3. Visibility: who may call
4. Private is not secret
5. State mutability: view, pure, payable
6. msg.sender and the constructor
7. Internal and external calls
8. Testing as another account

#### Lesson 5: Control Flow and Errors

*35 minutes.* Branch with if, else and the ternary, write loops knowing that every pass costs gas, stop a call with revert, require and custom errors, tell errors from panics, and test every failure with vm.expectRevert.

**Objectives**

- Write if/else chains, ternaries and bounded loops, and explain why a loop's cost grows with its passes
- Reject bad input with custom errors through revert and require, carrying the values that explain the failure
- Tell an error from a panic, and use assert only for conditions that can never be false
- Test each way a function fails with vm.expectRevert and an exact selector, encoded error, string or stdError value

**Outline**

1. Branches: if, else and the ternary
2. Loops, and why every pass costs gas
3. Stopping a call: revert and custom errors
4. require, with a custom error or a string
5. Panics and assert
6. A revert undoes the whole call
7. Testing reverts with vm.expectRevert

#### Lesson 6: Arrays, Strings and Bytes

*35 minutes.* Keep lists in fixed and dynamic storage arrays, grow and shrink them with push and pop, remove items with swap-and-pop, build fixed-size memory arrays, work with bytes and strings (joining, comparing by hash, measuring in bytes), and know what returning an array costs.

**Objectives**

- Declare fixed and dynamic storage arrays and use push, pop, length and indexing, recognising the out-of-bounds and empty-pop panics
- Remove an element with swap-and-pop and explain why delete alone leaves a gap
- Build a memory array with new T[](n), filling it in two passes when the size is not known
- Join strings with string.concat, compare them with keccak256, and measure them in bytes

**Outline**

1. Arrays in storage: fixed and dynamic
2. push, pop, length and out-of-bounds panics
3. Removing an element: delete and swap-and-pop
4. Arrays in memory
5. bytes and string
6. Returning arrays, and what it costs

#### Lesson 7: Mappings and Structs

*35 minutes.* Store values by key in mappings and nested mappings, group fields into structs kept in mappings and arrays, change them through storage references, track state with an enum whose zero value means "missing", list a mapping's keys with an array, and reset data with delete.

**Objectives**

- Read and write mappings and nested mappings, and explain why every key exists, with no length and no iteration
- Declare structs, store them in mappings and arrays, and change them through a storage reference
- Model a record's state with an enum whose first member stands for "does not exist"
- Keep an array of keys to list a mapping, and reset records with delete

**Outline**

1. Mappings: every key exists
2. Nested mappings
3. Structs in mappings and arrays
4. Change a struct through a storage reference
5. Enums as state, and the zero-value trap
6. Listing a mapping with an array of keys
7. delete

#### Lesson 8: Data Locations: storage, memory and calldata

*35 minutes.* Know where data lives and what it costs, tell a storage reference from a memory copy by the assignment rules, take external parameters as calldata, keep per-transaction state in transient storage, and read a contract's storage layout with forge inspect.

**Objectives**

- Predict whether an assignment copies data or creates a reference, for every pair of storage, memory and calldata
- Find and fix the bug of changing a memory copy of a struct that was meant to change storage
- Take external array and string parameters as calldata, and explain why it is cheaper and read-only
- Use a transient state variable for per-transaction state, and read slots with forge inspect storageLayout

**Outline**

1. Where data lives
2. Copies and references: the assignment rules
3. calldata for external parameters
4. Transient storage
5. Reading the storage layout

#### Lesson 9: Events and NatSpec

*35 minutes.* Record what happened with events that apps and indexers read, choose indexed parameters, test emitted events with vm.expectEmit and vm.recordLogs, and document a contract's public interface with NatSpec.

**Objectives**

- Declare and emit an event with up to three indexed parameters, and explain what goes into topics and what into data
- Test that a call emits the expected event with vm.expectEmit, and read raw logs with vm.recordLogs
- Decide what belongs in storage and what in an event, knowing that contracts cannot read logs
- Document public functions with NatSpec tags and read the userdoc and devdoc that the compiler produces

**Outline**

1. Why events exist
2. Declaring, emitting and testing an event
3. Topics and data
4. Reading raw logs with vm.recordLogs
5. NatSpec: documentation the compiler understands

#### Lesson 10: Modifiers and Access Control

*35 minutes.* Wrap functions in modifiers, write onlyOwner by hand, hand ownership over in two steps, give roles with a mapping, pause a contract, and see why tx.origin must never decide who may act.

**Objectives**

- Write modifiers with and without arguments and predict the order in which stacked modifiers run
- Restrict functions to an owner with a hand-written onlyOwner modifier and a custom error
- Transfer ownership in two steps and grant or revoke simple roles stored in a mapping
- Pause and unpause a contract, and explain why authorization uses msg.sender and never tx.origin

**Outline**

1. Modifiers wrap a function
2. An owner, by hand
3. Handing ownership over in two steps
4. Roles with a mapping, and pausing
5. Never authorize with tx.origin

#### Lesson 11: Receiving and Sending Ether

*40 minutes.* Accept ether with payable functions, receive and fallback, keep your own records of who paid what, send ether with call and check the result, avoid the deprecated transfer and send, and let users withdraw their own money.

**Objectives**

- Accept ether through payable functions and receive(), and predict whether receive, fallback or neither runs for a call
- Record each account's ether in a mapping and check it against balances in tests with vm.deal
- Send ether with a low-level call, revert with a custom error when it fails, and explain why transfer and send are deprecated
- Apply the pull pattern to withdrawals and refunds, updating state before sending

**Outline**

1. Payable functions and msg.value
2. receive and fallback
3. Sending ether with call
4. Why not transfer or send
5. Pull, don't push

#### Lesson 12: Putting It Together: a Complete Contract

*45 minutes.* Build a crowdfunding escrow from requirements to a reviewed, tested contract, using state, custom errors, events, modifiers and pull payments, and meet fuzz testing with bound and vm.assume.

**Objectives**

- Turn written requirements into state, errors, events and a small state machine
- Combine access control, checks-effects-interactions and pull payments in one contract
- Write a test suite that covers every path, including the refused ones
- Write fuzz tests with bound and vm.assume, and read a counterexample when one fails

**Outline**

1. Requirements
2. Designing the state
3. The contract
4. Unit tests
5. Fuzz testing
6. A review checklist

#### Practice labs

One small lab per lesson, offered at the end of the lesson and checked in the sandbox like any other lab.

| After the lesson | Practice lab | What the learner does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What Ethereum and Smart Contracts Are | Lantern Cruise Places | Run a finished contract for the first time, read what the test says about the value it returned, change the one number that is out of date, and submit. |
| Foundry and a First Contract | Cricket Club Scoreboard | Write the one missing function of a small contract that updates two state variables, then read what forge's tests report about the scoreboard after every ball. |
| Types, Variables and Units | Lavender Harvest Shares | Work out a lavender picker's share of a day's pay in wei, widening small integers before adding them, using an ether-unit constant, and multiplying before dividing. |
| Functions and Visibility | Mountain Hut Bunks | Write a function with two named return values that records its caller and calls a view function internally, tested from several accounts with vm.prank. |
| Control Flow and Errors | Blueberry Field Baskets | Price an order with a bounded loop and a floor, refuse bad orders with custom errors in a fixed order, and let only the farmer close the day. |
| Arrays, Strings and Bytes | Apiary Hive Roll | Keep a capped list of names in a storage array, check their length in bytes and their uniqueness by hash, remove with swap-and-pop, filter into a memory array and join strings. |
| Mappings and Structs | Costume Hire Wardrobe | Keep structs in a mapping with an array of keys, track their state with an enum, check permissions in a nested mapping, update records through storage references and retire them with delete. |
| Data Locations: storage, memory and calldata | Rowing Club Boat Log | Fix a struct update that changes only a memory copy, read batches from calldata, and cap the work done in one transaction with a transient counter. |
| Events and NatSpec | Sapling Planting Register | Declare an event with three indexed parameters, emit events with the right values in the right order, and prove it with vm.expectEmit and vm.recordLogs. |
| Modifiers and Access Control | Observatory Telescope Rota | Write guard modifiers for a role and a pause switch, put the missing guard back on the admin functions, and hand the directorship over in two steps. |
| Receiving and Sending Ether | Regatta Savings Jar | Accept ether through a payable function and receive(), refuse unknown calls in fallback(), and let members withdraw their own savings with a checked call. |
| Putting It Together: a Complete Contract | Harvest Supper Tickets | Finish a complete ticket sale with a stage machine, a seat limit, change and refunds paid by the pull pattern, and organiser-only cancellation, tested with fuzzing and a buyer that calls back in. |

#### Mock exam: Solidity Foundations Mock Exam

*24 questions · 20 minutes · pass mark 70%.* Ten questions drawn from the level's bank, from accounts and gas to types, functions, errors, storage, events and payments.

**Question 1** · One answer · `sol-basic-01`

A plain ether transfer uses 21,000 gas. When it is included, the base fee is 10 gwei per gas
and the sender offered a priority fee of 2 gwei per gas. What does the sender pay in fees, and
where does the money go?

- **✔ A. 252,000 gwei: the 210,000 gwei of base fee is burned and the 42,000 gwei of priority fee goes to the validator**
- B. 252,000 gwei, all of it paid to the validator that included the transaction
- C. 42,000 gwei: the sender pays only the priority fee, and the protocol covers the base fee
- D. 210,000 gwei: the priority fee is refunded because a plain transfer needs no tip

> **Why:** The fee is **gas used × (base fee + priority fee)**: 21,000 × (10 + 2) gwei = 252,000 gwei,
> which is 0.000252 ether. The two parts go to different places. The **base fee** is set by the
> protocol for each block and is **burned**, destroyed, so nobody receives it: 21,000 × 10 =
> 210,000 gwei. The **priority fee** is the tip that makes a validator want to include the
> transaction, and the validator keeps it: 21,000 × 2 = 42,000 gwei. The sender always pays
> the base fee; it is what makes the transaction valid at all. Nothing is refunded for being a
> simple transfer: what can be refunded is the part of a `maxFeePerGas` above base fee plus tip.

**Question 2** · Select all that apply · `sol-basic-02`

Which statements about Ethereum accounts are true? Choose all that apply.

- **✔ A. An externally owned account is controlled by whoever holds its private key; there is no way to reset a lost key**
- **✔ B. A contract account holds code and storage and has no private key; its code runs only when something calls it**
- C. A contract account can start a transaction by itself, for example every night at midnight, without anyone calling it
- D. A contract's state variable marked `private` cannot be read by anyone outside the contract

> **Why:** An **externally owned account** (EOA) is a key pair: the address is derived from the public
> key, and signing with the private key is the only proof of ownership, so a lost key means a
> lost account and a leaked key means anyone can empty it. A **contract account** has code and
> its own storage but no key, so it cannot sign: only an EOA starts a transaction, and a
> contract acts when a transaction (or another contract) calls it. Scheduled jobs need someone
> off chain to send the call. `private` only stops *other contracts* from reading a variable;
> every storage slot can be read from outside the chain, and lesson 04 reads a private door code
> with `vm.load`.

**Question 3** · One answer · `sol-basic-03`

`forge test` prints this line for a test of the swift tally from lesson 02:

```text
[FAIL: count after recording 12 and 5: 5 != 17] test_adds_each_record() (gas: 94305)
```

What does it tell you?

- **✔ A. An `assertEq` with the message `count after recording 12 and 5` failed: the contract returned 5 and the test expected 17**
- B. An `assertEq` failed: the contract returned 17 and the test expected 5
- C. The call to `record` reverted after 94,305 gas, so the count was never checked
- D. The test file did not compile, and forge shows the two line numbers where the error is

> **Why:** forge-std's `assertEq(actual, expected, message)` fails with the message first, then the two
> values with the **actual value first**: here `tally.count()` gave 5, while the test expected
> 12 + 5 = 17. That points at a `record` that overwrites the count (`count = seen;`) instead of
> adding to it. A revert would show its own reason instead, such as `panic: arithmetic underflow
> or overflow (0x11)`, and a compile error stops the run before any `[FAIL]` line. The gas is
> simply what the test used. This is why every check gets a message: in a hidden lab test, the
> message is all you see.

**Question 4** · One answer · `sol-basic-04`

```solidity
contract SwiftTallyTest is Test {
    SwiftTally tally;

    function setUp() public {
        tally = new SwiftTally();
    }

    function test_a() public {
        tally.record(5);
        assertEq(tally.count(), 5, "count in test_a");
    }

    function test_b() public {
        tally.record(2);
        assertEq(tally.count(), EXPECTED, "count in test_b");
    }
}
```

`record` adds its argument to `count`, which starts at 0. Which value of `EXPECTED` makes
`test_b` pass every time `forge test` runs both tests?

- **✔ A. 2**
- B. 7, because `test_a` runs first and its 5 is still in the tally
- C. 7 when `test_a` happens to run first and 2 otherwise, so no value works every time
- D. 0, because the change made by `record` is only visible in the next transaction

> **Why:** `setUp` runs before **each** test function, and each test starts from the state `setUp`
> left, with a freshly deployed `SwiftTally`. Nothing one test changes is seen by another, so
> the order in which forge runs them does not matter: `test_b` records 2 into a new tally and
> reads 2. Run in the sandbox, both tests pass with `EXPECTED` set to 2. The change is visible at
> once to the next call in the same test: there is no delay until a later transaction.

**Question 5** · One answer · `sol-basic-05`

```solidity
function total(uint8 morning, uint8 afternoon) public pure returns (uint16) {
    uint16 sum = morning + afternoon;
    return sum;
}
```

What happens when a test calls `total(200, 100)`?

- **✔ A. The call reverts with `panic: arithmetic underflow or overflow (0x11)`**
- B. It returns 300, because the result is stored in a `uint16`
- C. It returns 44, because the sum wraps around at 256
- D. It does not compile, because a `uint8` cannot be assigned to a `uint16`

> **Why:** The type of `morning + afternoon` is the type of its operands, `uint8`, whatever the variable
> it is stored in. 200 + 100 = 300 does not fit in a `uint8` (at most 255), and arithmetic has
> been **checked** since Solidity 0.8, so the addition reverts with panic code 0x11 before the
> widening to `uint16` happens. Wrapping to 44 is what an `unchecked` block would do. The
> assignment itself compiles: a `uint8` converts implicitly to the wider `uint16`. The fix is to
> widen first: `return uint16(morning) + afternoon;` returns 300.

**Question 6** · Select all that apply · `sol-basic-06`

Which statements about Solidity 0.8 are true? Choose all that apply.

- **✔ A. For `uint256 x = 300`, `uint8(x)` is 44, and the conversion does not revert**
- **✔ B. An `immutable` state variable can be assigned in the constructor, and never again after deployment**
- C. `uint256 constant OPENED = block.timestamp;` compiles and records the deployment time
- D. For `uint256 d = 3`, the expression `d days` is 259200

> **Why:** An explicit conversion to a smaller integer type **truncates silently**: it keeps the lowest
> 8 bits, and 300 − 256 = 44, with no error, so check the range yourself before narrowing a
> value that came from a user. An `immutable` is set during construction and is then copied into
> the deployed bytecode; assigning it in a function fails with `Cannot write to immutable here`.
> A `constant` must be known when the code is compiled, so `block.timestamp` is rejected with
> `Initial value for constant variable has to be compile-time constant.` (an `immutable` set in
> the constructor is the right tool). Unit suffixes apply only to literals: `d days` fails with
> `Expected ';' but got 'days'`, and the correct form is `d * 1 days`.

**Question 7** · One answer · `sol-basic-07`

```solidity
contract Caller {
    function whoCalls() public view returns (address) {
        return msg.sender;
    }

    function throughThis() external view returns (address) {
        return this.whoCalls();
    }
}
```

A test calls `throughThis()` after `vm.prank(address(0xADA))`. What does it return?

- **✔ A. The address of the `Caller` contract itself**
- B. `0xADA`, because `msg.sender` is the account that made the pranked call
- C. The test contract's address, because `vm.prank` only applies to `whoCalls`
- D. `address(0)`, because a view function called through `this` has no sender

> **Why:** `this.whoCalls()` is an **external call**: the contract sends a new message to itself, so
> inside `whoCalls` the immediate caller, `msg.sender`, is the `Caller` contract. Run in the
> sandbox, `throughThis()` returned the contract's address, while an internal call,
> `return whoCalls();` in another function, returned `0xADA`. `vm.prank` changes the sender of
> the next call from the test, which here is `throughThis`; it does not reach the call the
> contract makes itself. Use
> internal calls for helpers: they are cheaper and keep `msg.sender`.

**Question 8** · True or false · `sol-basic-08`

Declaring `uint256 private doorCode;` in a deployed contract stops anyone outside the contract
from finding out the door code.

- A. True
- **✔ B. False**

> **Why:** `private` is a rule for Solidity code: other contracts cannot read or call the member. It does
> not encrypt anything. Every storage slot of every contract can be read from outside the
> chain (`cast storage <address> <slot>`, or `vm.load` in a test, which printed `door code: 4321`
> in lesson 04), and the value was also visible in the transaction that set it. Never keep a
> password, key or answer in a contract, whatever its visibility.

**Question 9** · One answer · `sol-basic-09`

`Ferry` declares `error NoSeatsRequested();` and
`error NotEnoughSeats(uint256 available, uint256 requested);`, and starts with 40 seats left:

```solidity
function book(uint256 seats) external {
    if (seats == 0) revert NoSeatsRequested();
    require(seats <= seatsLeft, NotEnoughSeats(seatsLeft, seats));
    seatsLeft -= seats;
}
```

A test runs:

```solidity
vm.expectRevert(abi.encodeWithSelector(Ferry.NotEnoughSeats.selector, 40, 0));
ferry.book(0);
```

What does `forge test` report?

- **✔ A. `[FAIL: Error != expected error: NoSeatsRequested() != NotEnoughSeats(40, 0)]`**
- B. `[PASS]`: `book(0)` reverted, and `vm.expectRevert` only checks that the next call reverts
- C. `[FAIL: next call did not revert as expected]`, because 0 seats are always available
- D. `[PASS]`: both checks fail for 0 seats, and the test matches either error

> **Why:** `vm.expectRevert(bytes)` compares the **whole revert data**: the selector and every argument.
> `book` checks for zero seats first, so `book(0)` stops at `revert NoSeatsRequested()` and never
> reaches the `require`. The revert data is the selector of `NoSeatsRequested()`, not
> `NotEnoughSeats(40, 0)`, and forge reports both, as in the lesson's run. The call does revert,
> so "did not revert" is wrong, and a revert stops at the first failing check, so only one error
> is ever returned. The order of your checks is part of what callers and tests see.

**Question 10** · Select all that apply · `sol-basic-10`

Which of these revert with a **panic**, the built-in `Panic(uint256)` error, rather than with
an error you chose? Choose all that apply.

- **✔ A. `assert(seatsSold <= capacity);` when the condition is false**
- **✔ B. `return seatsLeft / cars;` when `cars` is 0**
- C. `require(msg.sender == captain, "only the captain");` when a stranger calls
- D. `require(seats <= seatsLeft, NotEnoughSeats(seatsLeft, seats));` when too many seats are asked for

> **Why:** A panic is raised when the code itself goes wrong: `assert` with a false condition gives
> `panic: assertion failed (0x01)`, and dividing by zero gives
> `panic: division or modulo by zero (0x12)`. Overflow (0x11), an index out of bounds (0x32) and
> `pop()` on an empty array (0x31) are other panics. `require` with a string reverts with the
> built-in `Error(string)`, and `require` with a custom error reverts with that error: both are
> errors you chose, to reject bad input. Correct code should never panic, which is why input is
> checked with `require` or `revert` and `assert` is kept for invariants.

**Question 11** · One answer · `sol-basic-11`

What does this expression return?

```solidity
bytes(unicode"Café Society").length
```

- **✔ A. 13**
- B. 12
- C. 24, because every character takes two bytes
- D. Nothing: it does not compile, because a string has no length

> **Why:** `string` has no `length`, but converting it with `bytes(...)` gives its UTF-8 bytes, which do.
> "Café Society" has 12 characters, but `é` takes two bytes in UTF-8, so the length is 13 (the
> lesson's test logged exactly that). ASCII characters take one byte each, so the answer is not
> 24. This is why a limit such as "names up to 16 bytes" must be stated and checked in bytes.
> Text outside ASCII also needs the `unicode"..."` prefix: `"Café"` alone fails with
> `Invalid character in string`.

**Question 12** · One answer · `sol-basic-12`

`titles` holds `["Moby-Dick", "Middlemarch", "Beloved", "Kindred"]`, and `remove(1)` runs:

```solidity
function remove(uint256 index) external {
    if (index >= titles.length) revert NoSuchTitle(index, titles.length);
    titles[index] = titles[titles.length - 1];
    titles.pop();
}
```

What does `titles` hold afterwards?

- **✔ A. `["Moby-Dick", "Kindred", "Beloved"]`**
- B. `["Moby-Dick", "Beloved", "Kindred"]`
- C. `["Moby-Dick", "", "Beloved", "Kindred"]`
- D. `["Kindred", "Moby-Dick", "Beloved"]`

> **Why:** This is **swap-and-pop**: the last element, Kindred, is copied over index 1 and `pop()` removes
> the old last slot. It costs the same whatever the length, but it changes the order, so an index
> someone saved earlier may now point at a different title. Keeping the order (Beloved before
> Kindred) needs every later element shifted down, which costs gas per element. A gap with an
> empty string is what `delete titles[1]` leaves: it resets one element and keeps the length.

**Question 13** · One answer · `sol-basic-13`

A tool shed declares its tools like this, and no tool has ever been listed:

```solidity
enum Status {
    Available,
    OnLoan
}

struct Tool {
    string name;
    Status status;
    address borrower;
    uint256 loans;
}

mapping(uint256 => Tool) public tools;

function borrow(uint256 id) external {
    Tool storage tool = tools[id];
    if (tool.status != Status.Available) revert NotAvailable(id, tool.status);
    tool.status = Status.OnLoan;
    tool.borrower = msg.sender;
    tool.loans += 1;
}
```

What happens when someone calls `borrow(99)`?

- **✔ A. It succeeds: tool 99 is recorded as on loan to the caller, with 1 loan**
- B. It reverts with `NotAvailable(99, 0)`, because tool 99 was never listed
- C. It reverts with a panic, because key 99 does not exist in the mapping
- D. It does not compile: a storage reference must point at an existing element

> **Why:** A mapping behaves as if every key exists, holding zero values. A tool never listed has
